Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 31, verse 1:

﴿Alif Lam Mim﴾

The discussion of its counterparts has already preceded at the beginning of Surah al-Baqarah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 31, verses 2–5:

[Page 140]
﴿These are the verses of the Wise Book.﴾ ﴿A guidance and a mercy for the good-doers,﴾ ﴿who establish the prayer, give the zakat, and are certain of the Hereafter.﴾ ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord, and those are the successful.﴾

If this surah was revealed because the Quraysh asked about Luqman and his son, then these verses up to His saying ﴿And We had certainly given Luqman wisdom﴾ [Luqman: 12] serve as an introduction explaining that the purpose of the Qur'an in narrating the story is the knowledge, wisdom and guidance contained in it, and that it is addressed to the believers, not to those who asked about it. Thus their question became a benefit for the believers.

The demonstrative "tilka" (those) refers to what will be mentioned in this surah. Its referent is implicit in the mind, anticipated for mention, as in His saying ﴿That is the Book﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2] at the beginning of al-Baqarah, and at the beginning of surahs al-Shu'ara', al-Naml and al-Qasas.

"Ayat al-Kitab" (the verses of the Book) is the predicate of the demonstrative. In the demonstrative there is an alert to the greatness of rank of those verses, through what the demonstrative indicates of distance, which is used to express elevated rank, and through what the attribution of the verses to the Book indicates, the Book being described as wise, as guidance, as mercy, as a means and as success.

"Al-Hakim" (the Wise) is a description of the Book in the sense of possessing wisdom, i.e., because it includes wisdom. Describing the Book as "wise" is like describing a man as wise, and for this reason it has been said that "al-Hakim" is an implicit metaphor (isti'arah makniyyah), or, in more elegant phrasing, a eloquent simile (tashbih baligh) to the wise man.

It is also possible that "al-Hakim" means "al-Muhkam" (the perfected), in the form of the passive participle, used as a description irregularly, as in their saying: "'asal 'aqid" (thick honey), because it is most firm and perfected, so there is no excess in it and nothing that does not add perfection to the soul.

In describing the Book with this attribute there is a fine opening (bara'at istihlal) for the purpose of mentioning the wisdom of Luqman. The description of the Book as "al-Hakim" was mentioned earlier at the beginning of surah Yunus.

"Hudan wa rahmah" (guidance and mercy) is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of "al-Kitab", and this is the reading of the majority. When the Book is the genitive complement, the justification for a hal coming from the genitive complement is that the Book was attributed to what is the name of its part; or it is a hal from "ayat". The governing element of the hal is the sense of the verb contained in the demonstrative.

Hamzah alone read it with the nominative "rahmatun", making "huda" a second predicate of the demonstrative.

The meaning of "al-muhsinin" (the good-doers) is those who do good deeds, the highest of which is faith, establishing the prayer and giving zakat. For this reason these three were singled out for mention after the general term "muhsinin", because they are the best of good deeds, although the good-doers also perform them along with other things.

The description of the Book as "rahmah" (mercy) after "huda" is because, since the purpose of this surah is the story of Luqman, He drew attention to the fact that mentioning the story is a mercy, for what it contains of manners and wisdom; for in that there is, beyond guidance, that one is cultivated with wisdom: ﴿And whoever is given wisdom has certainly been given much good﴾ [al-Baqarah: 269]. And "much good" is a mercy from Allah, exalted is He.

Zakat here means charity, and it was left to the aspirations of the Muslims, not restricted to a particular time or amount. The discussion of ﴿and they are certain of the Hereafter... they are the successful﴾ has already been covered at the beginning of surah al-Baqarah.

He used to travel for trade to the land of Persia, where he would obtain the lies of reports about their heroes in wars, filled with falsehoods. He would then recount them to the Quraysh in their evening gatherings, saying: "If Muhammad tells you the stories of 'Ad and Thamud, I will tell you the stories of Rustam, Isfandiyar and Bahram." Some exegetes said that al-Nadr used to buy books from the land of Persia containing the histories of their kings, and then narrated them to the Quraysh through someone who translated them for them. It was also said that the intended meaning of ﴿who buys idle talk﴾ is one who keeps singing slave-girls. Regarding such a matter this verse was revealed: ﴿Among people there are those who buy idle talk to lead astray from the path of God﴾ to the end of the verse. Abu 'Isa (al-Tirmidhi) said: "This is a strange hadith, narrated only through al-Qasim from Abu Umamah, and 'Ali ibn Yazid is weak in hadith. I heard Muhammad (i.e., al-Bukhari) say: 'Ali ibn Yazid is weak.'" End of quotation.

[p. 143]

Ibn al-'Arabi said in al-'Arida: Regarding the occasion of its revelation there are two views. The first is that it was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith. The second is that it was revealed concerning a man of the Quraysh (it was said he was Ibn Khatal) who bought a singing slave-girl, so people were occupied with her away from listening to the Prophet (ﷺ). End of quotation. The wording of the verse fits the story of al-Nadr ibn al-Harith most aptly.

The meaning of ﴿to lead astray from the path of God﴾ is that he does this in order to distract the Quraysh from listening to the Qur'an, for the Qur'an is a path that connects to God, that is, to the religion He intended. His aim was not mere diversion, but went beyond it to barring from the path of God. This adds to the denunciation of his action.

The majority of reciters read (yudilla) with a dammah on the yaʾ (meaning "to lead astray"). Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read it with a fathah on the yaʾ (yadilla, meaning "to go astray"), that is, so that he would increase in error upon error, since he did not content himself with disbelief for himself but began to spread his error among people. By this, the outcome of the two readings is one in meaning.

The phrase ﴿to lead astray from the path of God﴾ is connected to the verb "buys," and His words ﴿without knowledge﴾ are also connected to it. For the original principle regarding prepositional phrases is that they relate back to the verb upon which the sentence is built. The meaning is: he buys idle talk without knowledge, that is, without insight into the good of his own soul, since he exchanges falsehood for truth.

The pronoun in the accusative in (yattakhidhuha) refers back to "the path of God," since "path" (sabil) is feminine.

The majority read (wa-yattakhidhuha) with a dammah on the final vowel, in coordination with (yashtari), meaning: he occupies people with idle talk in order to divert them from the Qur'an, and takes the path of God as a mockery. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Hafs from 'Asim, Ya'qub and Khalaf read it in the accusative in coordination with (li-yudilla), meaning: he distracts them with idle talk in order to lead them astray, and in order that he take the religion of Islam as a mockery.

The outcome of the meaning is one in both readings, because both matters stem from his action and from his purpose. As for leading astray, the aspect of cause has been given preference, because it is the motivating reason for what he does.

[p. 144]

The word (huzu') is the verbal noun of (hazi'a bihi), meaning he mocked him, as in His words (they took the verses of God as a mockery).

Since the one who buys idle talk applies to al-Nadr ibn al-Harith and to those among the polytheists who listen to his tales, the threat against them is expressed in the plural form: ﴿Those, for them is a humiliating punishment﴾.

The demonstrative noun (ulaʾika, "those") was chosen to draw attention to the fact that the predicate that follows the demonstrative deserves it because of the attribute that precedes the demonstrative.

The sentence ﴿Those, for them is a humiliating punishment﴾ is a parenthetical clause (i'tiraid) placed between the two sentences: the sentence ﴿who buys﴾ and the sentence ﴿And when Our verses are recited to him﴾. Thus this is a coordination with the sentence (yashtari), etc. The full sense is: ﴿Among people there is one who buys﴾, etc., ﴿and when Our verses are recited to him, he turns away in arrogance﴾. Thus the relative pronoun is one, but it has two predicates: buying idle talk to lead astray, and arrogance when the verses of the Qur'an are recited to him.

His words ﴿are recited to him﴾ indicate that he is confronted with the conveying and the hearing of the Qur'an.

His words (wallā, "he turned away") are a figurative depiction of turning away from the verses of God, as in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Then he turned his back and strove﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 22].

And "arrogantly" (mustakbiran) is a circumstantial accusative (hal), meaning: it is a turning away of arrogance, not merely a turning away of neglecting good.

In this he is likened to one who does not hear the verses recited to him. The point of resemblance is the absence of being affected, even being affected in a way that would be followed by turning away, as with the affecting of al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah. The particle (ka'anna, "as if") is the light form of (ka'anna) and it occupies the position of a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in (mustakbiran).

The simile is repeated to reinforce it, though the manner differs: in the first, the non-hearing occurs while the faculty of hearing is intact; in the second, it occurs with the faculty of hearing lacking in strength. Thus he is likened secondly to one in whose ears is deafness, which is more specific than the meaning of ﴿as if he had not heard it﴾. A similar second simile is the verse of Labid:

Then they contended over a long shadow that sways, like the smoke of a fire kindled whose flames leap up,
Mixed with the sweet of a bush of 'arfaj, like the smoke of a fire whose fuel rises high.

The word (waqr) originally means heaviness, and it became a well-known metaphor for deafness, to the point that it equaled literal meaning. It was previously mentioned in His words ﴿and in their ears is deafness﴾ [al-An'am: 25] in Surat al-An'am.

Nafi' read (fi udhnayhi, "in his ears") with a sukun on the dhal for lightness because of the heaviness of the dual form. The rest read it with a dammah on the dhal, according to the original form.

Regarding such a matter this verse was revealed: ﴿Among people there are those who buy idle talk to lead astray from the path of God﴾ to the end of the verse. Abu 'Isa (al-Tirmidhi) said: "This is a strange hadith, narrated only through al-Qasim from Abu Umamah, and 'Ali ibn Yazid is weak in hadith. [p. 143]

Ibn al-'Arabi said in al-'Arida: Regarding the occasion of its revelation there are two views. The first is that it was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith. The second is that it was revealed concerning a man of the Quraysh (it was said he was Ibn Khatal) who bought a singing slave-girl, so people were occupied with her away from listening to the Prophet (ﷺ). End of quotation. The wording of the verse fits the story of al-Nadr ibn al-Harith most aptly.

The meaning of ﴿to lead astray from the path of God﴾ is that he does this in order to distract the Quraysh from listening to the Qur'an, for the Qur'an is a path that connects to God, that is, to the religion He intended. His aim was not mere diversion, but went beyond it to barring from the path of God. This adds to the denunciation of his action.

The majority of reciters read (yudilla) with a dammah on the yaʾ (meaning "to lead astray"). Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read it with a fathah on the yaʾ (yadilla, meaning "to go astray"), that is, so that he would increase in error upon error, since he did not content himself with disbelief for himself but began to spread his error among people. By this, the outcome of the two readings is one in meaning.

The phrase ﴿to lead astray from the path of God﴾ is connected to the verb "buys," and His words ﴿without knowledge﴾ are also connected to it. For the original principle regarding prepositional phrases is that they relate back to the verb upon which the sentence is built. The meaning is: he buys idle talk without knowledge, that is, without insight into the good of his own soul, since he exchanges falsehood for truth.

The pronoun in the accusative in (yattakhidhuha) refers back to "the path of God," since "path" (sabil) is feminine.

The majority read (wa-yattakhidhuha) with a dammah on the final vowel, in coordination with (yashtari), meaning: he occupies people with idle talk in order to divert them from the Qur'an, and takes the path of God as a mockery. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Hafs from 'Asim, Ya'qub and Khalaf read it in the accusative in coordination with (li-yudilla), meaning: he distracts them with idle talk in order to lead them astray, and in order that he take the religion of Islam as a mockery.

The outcome of the meaning is one in both readings, because both matters stem from his action and from his purpose. As for leading astray, the aspect of cause has been given preference, because it is the motivating reason for what he does.

[p. 144]

The word (huzu') is the verbal noun of (hazi'a bihi), meaning he mocked him, as in His words (they took the verses of God as a mockery).

Since the one who buys idle talk applies to al-Nadr ibn al-Harith and to those among the polytheists who listen to his tales, the threat against them is expressed in the plural form: ﴿Those, for them is a humiliating punishment﴾.

The demonstrative noun (ulaʾika, "those") was chosen to draw attention to the fact that the predicate that follows the demonstrative deserves it because of the attribute that precedes the demonstrative.

The sentence ﴿Those, for them is a humiliating punishment﴾ is a parenthetical clause (i'tiraid) placed between the two sentences: the sentence ﴿who buys﴾ and the sentence ﴿And when Our verses are recited to him﴾. Thus this is a coordination with the sentence (yashtari), etc. The full sense is: ﴿Among people there is one who buys﴾, etc., ﴿and when Our verses are recited to him, he turns away in arrogance﴾. Thus the relative pronoun is one, but it has two predicates: buying idle talk to lead astray, and arrogance when the verses of the Qur'an are recited to him.

His words ﴿are recited to him﴾ indicate that he is confronted with the conveying and the hearing of the Qur'an.

His words (wallā, "he turned away") are a figurative depiction of turning away from the verses of God, as in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Then he turned his back and strove﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 22].

And "arrogantly" (mustakbiran) is a circumstantial accusative (hal), meaning: it is a turning away of arrogance, not merely a turning away of neglecting good.

In this he is likened to one who does not hear the verses recited to him. The point of resemblance is the absence of being affected, even being affected in a way that would be followed by turning away, as with the affecting of al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah. The particle (ka'anna, "as if") is the light form of (ka'anna) and it occupies the position of a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in (mustakbiran).

The simile is repeated to reinforce it, though the manner differs: in the first, the non-hearing occurs while the faculty of hearing is intact; in the second, it occurs with the faculty of hearing lacking in strength. Thus he is likened secondly to one in whose ears is deafness, which is more specific than the meaning of ﴿as if he had not heard it﴾. A similar second simile is the verse of Labid:

Then they contended over a long shadow that sways, like the smoke of a fire kindled whose flames leap up,
Mixed with the sweet of a bush of 'arfaj, like the smoke of a fire whose fuel rises high.

The word (waqr) originally means heaviness, and it became a well-known metaphor for deafness, to the point that it equaled literal meaning. It was previously mentioned in His words ﴿and in their ears is deafness﴾ [al-An'am: 25] in Surat al-An'am.

[p. 145]

Nafi' read (fi udhnayhi, "in his ears") with a sukun on the dhal for lightness because of the heaviness of the dual form. The rest read it with a dammah on the dhal, according to the original form.

As a consequence of these actions by which he has been described, God commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to threaten him with a painful punishment. The use of the word "good news" here is an ironic metaphor (isti'arah tahakkumiyyah), as in the words of 'Amr ibn Kulthum:

"So we hastened to serve them hospitality, lest you revile us."

And al-Nadr was punished by the sword when he was killed by patient execution on the day of Badr. That is the punishment of this world, while the punishment of the Hereafter is more severe.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 31, verses 8–9:

﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds will have the Gardens of Bliss﴾ ﴿abiding therein forever. The promise of Allah is true, and He is the Mighty, the Wise.﴾

When He mentioned the punishment of those who lead astray from the way of Allah, He followed it with the glad tidings for the doers of good, those who are described as establishing the prayer, up to His saying: ﴿And those are the successful.﴾

The phrase "wa'da Allah" (the promise of Allah) is in the accusative as an absolute object (al-maf'ul al-mutlaq) standing in place of its verb (nasb: the grammatical case of the accusative). The word "haqqan" (truly) is in the accusative as an emphatic circumstantial qualifier (al-hal al-mu'akkidah) of the meaning of its governing verb, as was explained at the beginning of Surah Yunus. The placing of the two majestic names after the pronoun of majesty (Allah) serves to confirm His promise: since He is Mighty ('Aziz), the fulfillment of what He has promised cannot be beyond His capacity, and since He is Wise (Hakim), He does not err nor forget what He has promised. Therefore, the position of the clause "wa huwa al-'Aziz al-Hakim" is that of a concluding statement (tadhyil) with a more general application.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 31, verses 10–11:

﴿He created the heavens without pillars that you can see, and He cast into the earth firm mountains lest it shake with you, and He scattered therein every kind of moving creature. And We sent down water from the sky and caused to grow therein every noble pair.﴾ ﴿This is the creation of Allah. So show Me what those other than Him have created. Nay, the wrongdoers are in manifest error.﴾

It is a resumptive statement (isti'naf) giving evidence against those whose habit is turning away from the signs of Allah: that Allah is the Creator of the created things, so none other than Him deserves to be ascribed divinity. Thus the claim of divinity for other than Allah is the cause of their turning away from the signs of the Wise Book. For when they ascribed divinity to what creates nothing, they were like one who claims that the idols are similar to Allah, exalted is He, in His attributes; therefore this entails the negation of the attribute of wisdom from Him, just as it is negated from them. Hence the position of these verses is the position of "the evidence of the evidence" (dalil al-dalil), which is the situation expressed in the science of argumentation (ilm al-istidlal) with precision, namely mentioning a thing together with its evidence and the evidence of that evidence.

The address in His words "you see" (taraunaha) and "with you" (bikum) is to the polytheists. His words "Allah is He who raised the heavens without pillars that you can see" [al-Ra'd: 2] have already preceded in Surat al-Ra'd, and His words "and cast into the earth firm mountains lest it shake with you" have preceded at the beginning of Surat al-Nahl, and the meaning is "fearing that it shake with you," or "so that it does not shake you," as was explained there.

His words "and He scattered therein every kind of moving creature" have preceded in Surat al-Baqarah, along with "and the changing of the winds" [al-Baqarah: 164].

His words "We sent down water from the sky" are a parallel to His words in Surat al-Baqarah, "And what Allah sent down from the sky of water" [al-Baqarah: 164], and to His words in Surat al-Ra'd, "He sent down from the sky water, and valleys flowed" [al-Ra'd: 17].

The shift from the third person to the first person in His words "We sent down" is for the sake of attention to this blessing, which is the most frequently encountered among people.

The pronoun in "therein" refers to the earth.

The "zawj" (pair) is the kind (sinf). It has preceded in His words, exalted is He, "So We brought forth thereby pairs of varied plants" [Ta-Ha: 53] in Surat Ta-Ha, and His words "And it grew from every beautiful pair" [al-Hajj: 5] in Surat al-Hajj.

The "karim" is the precious of its kind; it has preceded at His words, exalted is He, "Indeed, there has been delivered to me a noble letter" [al-Naml: 29] in Surat al-Naml.

Within the proofs of the attribute of wisdom, a favour has been inserted by the benefits that this contains for creatures, through His words "lest it shake with you" and "He scattered therein every kind of moving creature." Among the moving creatures scattered are those from which people benefit by eating the flesh of their domestic and wild animals, and by benefiting from their milk, wool, hides, horns and teeth, and by riding them and adorning themselves with them at their stables, in their morning and evening going out. Then, from the blessing of the benefits of plants: grain, fruit, pasture and truffles. And since the seas are part of the earth, the benefit includes the creatures of the sea. So Allah, just as He originated the craft, has lavished the blessing, and has shown us the traces of wisdom and mercy.

Its sentence "This is the creation of Allah" to its end is the conclusion of the argument from the creation of the heavens, the earth, the mountains, the creatures and the sending down of rain. The demonstrative noun refers to what His words "He created the heavens" up to His words "every noble pair" contain. Bringing it in the singular is by interpreting it as "the thing mentioned."

The shift from the first person to the third person in "the creation of Allah" is a shift (iltifat) to increase the explicitness that the address comes from the side of Allah, by the indication of His words "This is the creation of Allah." Likewise, the shift from the first person to the third person in His words "What have those other than Him created" is a shift to observe the return to the third person in His words "the creation of Allah."

It is permissible that the seeing in His words "show Me" (fa-aruni) be cognitive ('ilmiyyah), that is, "inform Me," with the verb suspended from operating by the interrogative "what" (madha).

It is then necessary that "fa-aruni" be sarcastic (tahakkum), because it is not possible for them to contend against Allah, in addition to the matter being used for challenge (ta'jiz). But sarcasm takes precedence, for the certainty that they cannot contend against Allah comes before the certainty of their inability to specify a created thing which other than Allah created, a theoretical certainty.

The formation of the challenge command from the root of visual seeing is stronger in challenge, because it requires their conviction by bringing forth something which they claim their gods created. This is like the saying of Hutaith ibn Ya'fur al-Nahshali, or it is said Hatim al-Ta'i:

"Show me a steed that died of emaciation, perhaps I may see what you adorn, or a miserly one immortalized."

That is, bring me a steed that died of emaciation and show it to me, perhaps I may see the like of what you saw.

The Arabs intend by such a purpose the visual seeing, and therefore it is common to say: "What my eye has seen," and "Look, do you see?" Imru' al-Qays said:

"So by Allah, the two eyes of whoever sees dispersal, more scattered and more distant than the separation of al-Muhassab."

The application of the relative pronoun of rational beings to the idols is a reckoning with the polytheists, since they count them as rational.

"Min dunihi" is the relative clause's complement; "dun" is a metonymy for "other than," and "min" is a preposition governing a place noun, in the manner of an addition, to emphasize the connection with the adverbial phrase.

"Bal" is for a transitional turning away (idrab intiqali) from the purpose of disputation to the purpose of recording their error, that is, in their belief in the divinity of the idols, as is said in debate: "Leave this aside," and he moved on to such-and-such.

"The wrongdoers" are the polytheists. "Manifest error" is the atrocious disbelief, because they turned away from the call of Islam to the truth, and that is error, and they associated with Allah others in divinity, and that is atrocious disbelief.

The particle of location has been brought to convey that error encompasses them in all their conditions, that is, the intensity of its being attached to them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 31, verse 12 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And We had certainly given Luqman wisdom, [saying], "Be grateful to Allah. And whoever is grateful, his gratitude is only for [the benefit of] himself. And whoever is ungrateful - then indeed, Allah is Free of need and Praiseworthy."﴾.

The conjunction "wa" (and) joins the story of Luqman to the story of al-Nadr ibn al-Harith mentioned earlier, in His saying, ﴿And among the people is one who purchases idle talk to mislead [others] from the way of Allah﴾ [Luqman: 6], in terms of its including the strange state of his deviation, from his concern with idle talk in order to mislead from the way of Allah and take the way of Allah in mockery; and in terms of the story of Luqman including the strange state of Luqman in guidance and wisdom. Thus they are two opposing states. The consideration of the story of al-Nadr being brought as an introduction and a preface to the intended matter is set aside, because when the speech in the introduction became lengthy, it departed from the usual pattern of introductions into things that are intended in themselves. Therefore it was joined in the manner of stories and was not separated in the manner of conclusions following their premises. Multiple considerations may apply to a single style, and the eloquent speaker chooses among them, as in His saying, ﴿They inflict upon you the worst torment, slaughtering your sons﴾ [al-Baqarah: 49] in Surat al-Baqarah, and ﴿and they slaughter your sons﴾ [Ibrahim: 6] in Surat Ibrahim. The opening of the story with the two emphatic particles, the oath particle lam and "qad", serves to announce that it is a report of an important, actual matter.

"Luqman" is the name of a wise, righteous man. Most of the reports about him, which some of them support one another although their chains of transmission are weak, indicate that he was of the blacks; it is said that he was from the land of Nubia, and it is said that he was from Abyssinia.

He is not Luqman ibn 'Ad, who is the subject of the well-known proverb ("one of Luqman's vulture-mothers" - ihda hazziyat Luqman), and who was mentioned by Abu al-Muhawwash al-Asadi or Yazid ibn 'Umar, [the verse] "You see him wandering the horizons, greedy to eat the head of Luqman ibn 'Ad" (ta-rahu yutawwifu al-afaqa hirsan li-ya'kula ra'sa Luqmana ibn 'Ad). He is known by that name, Luqman the owner of vultures, and he had a son named Luqaym. Some have mentioned that the name of his father was Ba'ura', so it occurred to some authors that he is the one named in the books of the Jews as Balaam ibn Ba'ura', whose story is mentioned in chapters 22 and 23 of the Book of Numbers. Perhaps this is a mistake, because that Balaam was a man from the people of Midian who was a prophet in the time of Moses, peace be upon him. Perhaps the confusion came from the coincidence of the father's name, or from the assumption that Balaam is synonymous in meaning with Luqman, since Balaam is from "bala'" (swallowing) and Luqman is from "laqm" (gulping), so the Arabs may have named him with something synonymous with his name in Hebrew.

The early scholars differed as to whether Luqman mentioned in the Qur'an was a wise man or a prophet. The majority said: he was a wise, righteous man. Malik relied on the second in the Muwatta', so he mentioned him twice in the Jami' of the Muwatta' with the description "Luqman the Wise", and this indicates that he was well known for that among the scholars of Madinah. Ibn 'Atiyyah mentioned that Ibn 'Umar said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: "Luqman was not a prophet, but he was a servant who reflected much, of good certainty, who loved Allah, so Allah loved him and bestowed upon him wisdom." It appears from the verses mentioned in his story here that he was not a prophet, because he was not favored with revelation nor with the speech of the angels. Restricting the statement to his being given wisdom alludes to his being inspired with wisdom and speaking it. Also, when his teaching to his son was mentioned, Allah said, ﴿while he was advising him﴾ [Luqman: 13], and this indicates that it was instruction, not the conveying of legislation.

'Ikrimah and al-Sha'bi held that Luqman was a prophet, and the word "wisdom" permits this view, because wisdom is used for prophethood in much of the Qur'an, as in His saying about Dawud, ﴿And We gave him wisdom and decisive speech﴾ [Sad: 20]. Wisdom in His saying, ﴿And whoever is given wisdom has certainly been given much good﴾ [al-Baqarah: 269] has been explained as including prophethood. Wisdom is (knowledge of the realities of things as they are), and its highest form is prophethood, because it is knowledge of realities protected from being contrary to what they are in fact, since prophethood is received from Allah, from whose knowledge nothing is hidden.

It will come that the mention of His saying, ﴿And We have enjoined upon man [care] for his parents﴾ [Luqman: 14] within the speech of Luqman supports this view.

The people of tafsir and history mentioned that he was in the time of Dawud. Some of them say that he was the son of the sister of Ayyub or his maternal cousin, so it is established that he lived in the land of Israel. Some of them mentioned that he was a slave whom his master freed. Ibn Kathir mentioned from Mujahid that Luqman was a judge among the Children of Israel in the time of Dawud, peace be upon him, but no mention of that is found in the books of the Israelites.

It was said that he was a shepherd of sheep; it was said that he was a carpenter; and it was said that he was a tailor. In the tafsir of Ibn Kathir, from Ibn Wahb, Luqman was a slave of the Banu al-Hisḥas, and the Banu al-Hasḥas are from the Arabs; and among their slaves was Suhaym, the slave poet, the mukhadram, who was killed during the reign of 'Uthman.

The wisdom of Luqman is related in his sayings which speak of the realities of conditions and bring hidden things near through the best of examples. People of moral education and people of goodness have been concerned with it. The Qur'an mentioned from it what is in this surah, and Malik mentioned from it two statements in the Jami' of the Muwatta', and he mentioned a wise saying of his in the book Jami' al-'Utbiyyah, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal mentioned some of it in his Musnad. We do not know of a book that collected the wisdom of Luqman.

In the tafsir of al-Qurtubi, Wahb ibn Munabbih said: "I read from the wisdom of Luqman more than ten thousand chapters." Perhaps this, if it is authentically from Wahb ibn Munabbih, was an exaggeration in the abundance.

Luqman was known among the elite of the Arabs. Ibn Ishaq said in the Sirah: "Suwayd ibn al-Samit, a brother of the Banu 'Amr ibn 'Awf, came to Makkah for pilgrimage or for 'umrah, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ approached him and invited him to Islam. Suwayd said to him: 'Perhaps what you have is like what I have.' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to him: 'And what do you have?' He said: 'The Majallat Luqman.' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to him: 'Present it to me.' So he presented it to him, and he said: 'This speech is good, but what I have is better than this: it is a Qur'an which Allah has revealed.'" Ibn Ishaq said: "He came to Madinah and did not stay long before the Khazraj killed him, and his killing is said to have been on the day of Bu'ath. Some men of his people used to say: 'We see that he was killed while he was a Muslim,' and his people used to call him al-Kamil." End of quote. In al-Isti'ab of Ibn 'Abd al-Barr: "I am doubtful about his Islam, as others have doubted."

It has already been mentioned at the beginning of the discussion of this surah that the Quraysh asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about Luqman and his son, and this indicates that he was known to the Arabs.

By the time of writing this tafsir, there have reached me thirty-eight wise sayings of Luqman transmitted beyond what is mentioned in this verse, and we will mention them upon finishing the tafsir of these verses.

Al-iytа' (giving) means bestowing, and it is used here metaphorically for inspiration or revelation.

Luqman is a proper name whose root is Arabic, derived from "laqm" (gulping). The more apparent view is that the Arabs Arabicized it with a form close to the words of their language, as is their custom, just as they Arabicized Saul as Talut. It is diptote (not declined with tanwin) because of the added alif and nun, not because of foreignness.

The definition of wisdom has already been given at His saying, ﴿He gives wisdom to whom He wills﴾ [al-Baqarah: 269] in Surat al-Baqarah, and at His saying, ﴿Invite to the way of your Lord with wisdom﴾ [al-Nahl: 125] in Surat al-Nahl.

The "an" (that) in His saying, ﴿that be grateful to Allah﴾ is explanatory (tafsiriyyah), and it is not an explanation of the verb "We gave", because that verb has taken as its object wisdom itself. Thus "an" explains "wisdom", on the basis that wisdom here is statements that were revealed to him or inspired into him, so there is in "wisdom" the meaning of speech without its letters, and therefore it is suitable to be explained by the explanatory "an", just as "hajah" (need) was explained in the verse of the poet, whose identity is unknown (and it is among the evidences of Arabic grammar):

If you two carry a need for me, its burden is light, you two deserve a favor and a hand from me for it,
that you two recite to me Asma', woe to you, [the greeting of peace] from me, and that you not inform anyone.

The Sufis and the philosophers of illumination (Hukama' al-Ishraq) consider the inspirations of the chosen ones to be a proof, and they call them inspiration (ilham).

A great number of our scholars inclined to this. Qutb al-Din al-Shirazi said in the preface of his commentary on al-Miftah: "As to what follows: there has been cast upon me, by way of warning, from the presence of the Mighty King, in the tongue of inspiration, only like a delusion of the delusions, which has caused me to turn away from the abode of deception and to turn back to the abode of joy," etc.

The first thing Luqman was taught of wisdom was wisdom concerning himself: Allah commanded him to be grateful for what surrounds him of Allah's blessings, among which is the blessing of being chosen by being given wisdom and being prepared for it by his capacity for it. This is the head of wisdom, because it includes considering the signs of his own self and its reality before considering the realities of things and before undertaking to guide others. The most important consideration of his own reality is the awareness of his existence in a complete state, the awareness of its Originator and the Source of perfection upon him, and all of that necessitates thanking its Originator for that.

Also, thanking Allah is part of wisdom, since wisdom calls for knowing the realities of things as they are, for the purpose of acting according to knowledge. The wise person spreads those realities among people according to their capacities, through legislation at times and admonition at other times, and teaches the one who receives it, while urging them to act on what they have learned. That action is part of gratitude, since gratitude has been defined as the servant's directing all the blessings and favors that Allah has bestowed upon him toward what they were created for. Thus the gratitude to Allah is the most important of righteous deeds, and therefore it is the head of wisdom, because among wisdom is giving precedence to knowledge of what is most beneficial over knowledge of what is lesser. Gratitude is the origin of perfections in knowledge, and its end in action.

To draw attention to this meaning, Allah followed the commanded gratitude with an explanation that its benefit returns to the one who is grateful, not to the one thanked, by His saying, ﴿And whoever is grateful, his gratitude is only for [the benefit of] himself﴾, because the effects of gratitude to Allah are perfections attained by the grateful person, and they do not benefit the one thanked in any way, since He, glory be to Him, is free of need from the gratitude of the grateful. For this reason it was expressed in the form of a conditional, to establish the connection between the content of the condition and the content of the consequence, since the conditional is more indicative of this than a simple statement.

The form of restriction (hasr) was used to confine the benefit of gratitude to the grateful person, by His saying, ﴿his gratitude is only for himself﴾, meaning he is not grateful except for the benefit of himself, and the lam of causation indicates benefit. This was made clearer by conjoining its opposite, in His saying, ﴿And whoever is ungrateful - then indeed, Allah is Free of need and Praiseworthy﴾, to convey that turning away from gratitude after perceiving it is ingratitude for the blessing, and that Allah is free of need of its gratitude, unlike the case of created beings, for gratitude brings them benefits among their own kind that draw to them the advantages of obedience, or help, or enrichment, or other benefits of gratitude for those thanked, according to the differences of their ranks; whereas Allah is free of need of all of that. And He is Praiseworthy, meaning He is abundantly praised by the tongue of the state of all existing things, even the state of the disbeliever in Him, as He said, ﴿And to Allah prostrates whoever is in the heavens and the earth, willingly and unwillingly﴾ [al-Ra'd: 15].

Among the eloquence of the Qur'an and its wondrous conciseness is that His saying, ﴿that be grateful to Allah﴾, comprised both the principle of the wisdom that Luqman was given and the command to thank Him for that. Thus His saying, ﴿that be grateful to Allah﴾, gathered both the guidance to gratitude together with the beginning of the matter for which gratitude is due, as an alert to hastening to gratitude upon the arrival of a blessing.

The reason the turning away from gratitude is paired with God's description as "Praiseworthy" is that praise (ḥamd) and gratitude (shukr) are closely related. A hadith says, "Praise is the head of gratitude." Since among God's names there is no name derived from the root of shukr except al-Shakūr, which means shākir (One who gives thanks), that is, He gives thanks to His servants for their worship of Him, the verse uses the name Ḥamīd here instead.

The verb yashkuru is in the present tense (muḍāriʿ) to indicate that the worthiness of gratitude is renewed continually.

The lām in ﴿أنِ اشْكُرْ لِلَّهِ﴾ ("Give thanks to God") is attached to the object of shukr. It is a lām whose addition with the root shukr is obligatory (multazim), for emphasis and reinforcement. It has already been discussed in His words ﴿وَاشْكُرُوا لِي﴾ ("and be grateful to Me") [al-Baqarah: 152] in Sūrat al-Baqarah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 31, verse 13:

﴿And [mention] when Luqman said to his son, while he was advising him: "O my son, do not associate anything with Allah. Indeed, association [with Him] is a great injustice."﴾

This is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon the clause ﴿We gave Luqman wisdom﴾ [Luqman: 12], because the waw (conjunction) stands in place of the verb. Thus the content of this clause explains part of the wisdom that Luqman was given. The implied sense is: "And We gave him wisdom when he said to his son," so at the time of saying that to his son he had been given wisdom, and that statement was undoubtedly of wisdom. And in every state that issues from him in which there is wisdom, he has been given wisdom in it.

"Idh" (إذْ, "when") is an adverb (zarf) related to the implied verb indicated by the conjunctive waw; that is, the implied sense is: "And We gave him wisdom when he said to his son." This is a transition from describing him with the wisdom of guidance (ihtida') to describing him with the wisdom of guidance and direction (huda wa al-irshad). It is also permissible that "idh qala" be an adverb related to a deleted verb "udhkur" (remember).

The purpose of mentioning the circumstance with his words ﴿while he was advising him﴾ is to indicate that this statement was made because his son was engaged in associating partners with Allah. The majority of the exegetes have said that Luqman's son was a polytheist, and Luqman kept advising him until he believed in Allah alone. Advice (wa'z) is a rebuke combined with intimidation, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So turn away from them, admonish them, and speak to them a far-reaching word within themselves﴾ [al-Nisa': 63]. The one being rebuked is identified by the complement of the verb of admonition, so it is determined that the rebuke here is against associating partners with Allah. Perhaps Luqman's son adhered to the religion of his people, the Sudanese; then, when Allah opened to Luqman with wisdom and monotheism, his son refused to follow him, so he kept advising him until he adopted monotheism. Luqman's settling in the city of David does not necessitate that his family followed the religion of the Jews.

The original form of prohibition against something is that it occurs at the time one is engaged in the forbidden thing or when one is approaching engagement with it. The principle is that one does not forbid something that is absent from the one being forbidden. The exegetes have mentioned disagreement over the name of Luqman's son, but there is no need for it.

In this admonition Luqman gathered the foundations of the Sharia, which are: the beliefs (i'tiqadat), the deeds (a'mal), the etiquette of dealing (adab al-mu'amala), and the etiquette of the self (adab al-nafs).

Opening the admonition with addressing the one being advised, although directing speech to him already suffices for his attention since he is present to the address, the vocative (nida') is used figuratively to seek the presence of mind for comprehending the speech, and this is from the concern for the purpose toward which the speech is directed, as was mentioned earlier at His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿O my father, indeed I saw eleven stars﴾ [Yusuf: 4], and His saying ﴿O my son, do not relate your vision﴾ [Yusuf: 5] in Surat Yusuf, and His saying ﴿When the disciples said, "O Jesus, son of Mary, can your Lord send down to us a table from the heaven?"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 112] in Surat al-'Uqud, and His, exalted is He, saying ﴿When he said to his father, "O my father, why do you worship that which does not hear and does not see?"﴾ [Maryam: 42] in Surat Maryam.

"Bunayya" is the diminutive of "ibn" (son) when attached to the first-person ya' (my), therefore the ya' is vowelled with kasra. The majority read the ya' of "bunayyi" with a kasra and shadda. Its original form is: "ya bunayyiyi" with three ya's, since its original root is "ya bunayyawi," because the word "ibn" has a waw as its third radical, whose deletion is obligatory. When it was diminutivized, it was restored to its origin. Then, when the diminutive ya' came together, vowelless, before the waw of the word, which is vowelled by the case-ending vowel, the waw was changed into ya' because of their similarity and they were assimilated. When it was addressed while attached to the first-person ya', the first-person ya' was deleted, because deletion of it in the vocative is permissible and because of the dislike of repeating similar forms. The deleted ya' was indicated by obligating the kasra in the three case states, because the kasra is evidence of the first-person ya'. This was discussed in Surat Yusuf.

The diminutive here serves to place the grown addressee in the position of a little one, as a metaphor for compassion toward him and affection for him. In the context of admonition and counsel, it is a hint and a metaphor for sincerity of advice and love of good, so it contains encouragement to comply with the admonition.

Luqman began his son's admonition by asking him to desist from associating partners with Allah, because the soul that is prepared for purification and perfection must first be cleared of the beginnings of corruption and misguidance, for the reform of belief is the foundation for the reform of action. The root of corruption of belief is one of two matters: materialism (al-dahriyya) and associationism (al-ishrak). So his saying ﴿do not associate﴾ affirms the existence of a deity and nullifies that He has a partner in His divinity.

Hafs, from 'Asim, read in the three places in this surah "ya bunayya" with a fatha on the ya' and shadda, on the assumption of: "ya bunayya" with an alif, and this is the fifth dialect regarding the vocative attached to the first-person ya'; then the alif was deleted and the fatha was left in its place. This is a transmitted (sama'i) usage.

The clause ﴿Indeed, association is a great injustice﴾ is a justification for the prohibition against it and an emphasis on its gravity, for it is an injustice against the rights of the Creator; a person's injustice to himself when he places himself in the abyss of servitude to the lowliest inanimate objects; an injustice against the people of true faith when it incites their persecution and harm; and an injustice to the realities of things by reversing them and corrupting their relations.

This is part of Luqman's speech, as is the apparent context, and Hadith in Sahih Muslim indicates it, from 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, who said: "When the verse ﴿Those who believe and do not mix their belief with injustice﴾ [al-An'am: 82] was revealed, it was difficult for the companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and they said: 'Which of us does not wrong himself?' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'It is not as you think; rather it is as Luqman said to his son: ﴿O my son, do not associate anything with Allah. Indeed, association is a great injustice.﴾'"

Ibn 'Atiyya permitted that the clause ﴿Indeed, association is a great injustice﴾ be part of the speech of Allah, Exalted is He, i.e., parenthetical between the words of Luqman. It is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that when they said that, Allah, Exalted is He, revealed ﴿Indeed, association is a great injustice﴾. Consider who narrated this and the degree of its authenticity.

[p. 157]

If we take the view that Luqman was not a prophet who conveyed a message from God, but a wise man who gave guidance, then this statement is a parenthetical insertion (*i'tiraḍ*, a phrase placed between parts of a discourse) between the two statements of Luqman. The form of this statement is cast in the style of conveying a message and of quoting one of God's sayings. The pronouns are pronouns of majesty. The context of Luqman's prohibition of his son from associating partners with God, and the description of that act as grave, brought this about. God thus mentioned this to reinforce what is in Luqman's counsel of prohibition against shirk, generalizing the prohibition to persons and circumstances, lest someone suppose that the prohibition applies only to Luqman's son or only to certain situations. God related that He had enjoined this on every human being, and that there is no leniency in it, even in the most difficult circumstances, which is the situation of parents striving to make their children associate partners with God.

A better explanation of the connection is this: when He related Luqman's counsel to his son, which was the thanks due to God by declaring Him free of association in divinity, God showed that He, may He be exalted, has the greater claim to bounty over His servants, in that He enjoined sons to be dutiful to their fathers. Thus the bounty upon Luqman was included in the general sense, as a reward for his observance of God's right at the outset of his admonition to his son. So God is more precedent in beneficence toward those who did good by observing His right. This interpretation is strengthened by the linking of thanks to God with thanks to the parents in the command.

If we take the view that Luqman was a prophet, then this statement is among what Luqman conveyed to his son, and it is among what he was given of revelation. It would have been related in the manner in which it was revealed to him, similar to the style of His saying ﴿Give thanks to God﴾ [Luqman: 12]. This possibility is more fitting to the context of the discourse, and it is preferred by the difference in style between it and the two verses of Surat al-'Ankabut and Surat al-Ahqaf, because what is here is a narration of what preceded in another community, whereas the other two are a fresh address to this community. It has been reported that when Luqman conveyed this to his son, he said to him: "God has been pleased with me for you, so He did not enjoin you upon me; and He was not pleased with you for me, so He enjoined you upon me."

The purpose of this statement is His saying ﴿But if they strive with you to make you associate with Me﴾ to the end of the verse, and what precedes it is a preparation for it and an establishment of the obligation of kindness to parents, so that the prohibition against obeying them becomes, in effect, a command to associate partners with God, a prohibition against it in the circumstance most deserving of obedience. Thus the prohibition against shirk in lesser circumstances is understood by implication of the discourse (*fahwa al-khiṭab*), together with the fine incorporation (*idmaj*) fitting to Luqman's wisdom, whether this is from Luqman's words or from God's, may He be exalted.

On both interpretations, what some exegetes have held is not good: that this verse was revealed concerning the case of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas's conversion to Islam and his mother's displeasure. This is because it does not fit the context, and because it has already been mentioned that the parallel of this verse in Surat al-'Ankabut was revealed about that. And it is that verse which is appropriate to the occasion of revelation, for it is free of the descriptions in which there is tenderness toward the mother, unlike this one. There is no basis for two verses to be revealed on a single purpose at different times. The one enjoined will be explained later.

*Al-wahn* (weakness), with the *ha'* vowelless, is the verbal noun of *wahana*, *yahinu*, from the pattern of *ḍaraba*. It is said also *wahan*, with the *ha'* vocalized, as the verbal noun of *wahana*, *yuhinu*, like *wajila*, *yawjalu*. It means weakness and lack of strength to bear something.

*Wahnan* is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) of *ummuhu* (his mother), for emphasis on her weakness, to the point that she is as if she were weakness itself, i.e., being weak in carrying him. *'Ala wahnin* is an attribute of *wahnan*, i.e., a weakness befalling upon weakness, as one says *raja'a 'awdan 'ala bad'in* ("he returned repeatedly to the beginning"), when one resumes a task he had finished and returns to it, i.e., after a beginning. Or *'ala* has the sense of *ma'a* (with), as in the verse of al-Ahwas:

*Inni 'ala ma qad 'alimta muḥassadun*
*anmi 'ala al-baghḍa'i wal-shana'ani*

Indeed, despite what you know, I am envied;
I grow up amid hatred and enmity.

The pregnancy of a woman is accompanied by fatigue from the weight of the fetus in the womb, and by weakness from the diversion of her blood to nourishing the fetus. That weakness continues to increase as the period of pregnancy lengthens. Therefore it is undoubtedly a weakness upon weakness.

The clause ﴿his mother bore him in weakness upon weakness﴾ is in the position of a reason (ta'lil) for the command concerning parents, intended to reinforce that command, because the stating of the reason for a ruling affirms it, and because the content of this clause stirs in the child's soul the motive to be dutiful to his mother, and this leads to dutifulness to his father too.

The reason for the command concerning the parents was stated by mentioning circumstances specific to one of them, namely the mother, relying on the fact that this condition requires the command concerning the father too, by analogy (*qiyas*). The father encounters hardships and fatigue in providing for the mother, so that she may be free to attend to the child during the period of his care. Then he takes charge of his upbringing and protection until he reaches his maturity and no longer needs support, as God, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And say: My Lord, have mercy on them both as they raised me when I was small﴾ [al-Isra': 24]. Thus He combined them in raising the child in his infancy, which concerns his preservation and the completion of his upbringing. So when the condition that requires dutifulness to the mother is mentioned here, namely carrying and nursing, it serves as an alert to the condition of the father that requires dutifulness to him, in proportion to what the same cause requires in both, in strength and weakness. The difference in the strength of the quality that justifies the extension of the ruling does not invalidate the analogy between the analogue and its base. This analogy is indicated by the joining of the two in the command to be grateful, immediately after it, in His saying ﴿Give thanks to Me and to your parents﴾ and His saying ﴿and keep them company in this world with kindness﴾.

From this wondrous arrangement is achieved the fulfilment of the right of conciseness (*ījāz*).

As for the preponderance of the mother in this matter when the demands of dutifulness conflict in a way in which reconciliation is not possible, Ibn 'Atiyyah said in his exegesis: "God, in this verse, placed the mother and the father in the same rank of the command concerning them, then singled out the mother by mention of the stage of carrying and the stage of nursing, so that the mother has three degrees and the father one. This resembles the saying of the Messenger ﷺ when a man said to him: 'Who is most deserving of my good companionship?' He said: 'Your mother.' He said: 'Then who?' He said: 'Your mother.' He said: 'Then who?' He said: 'Your mother.' He said: 'Then who?' He said: 'Your father.' So he was given a quarter of the dutifulness." This statement, similar to it, is attributed to Ibn Battal in his commentary on Sahih al-Bukhari.

It is not hidden that the context of the hadith is to affirm dutifulness to the mother, since failing in the due obligation to the mother may occur on the part of the son, relying on the gentleness he receives from her, unlike the case of the father, who is strong, and whose children are wary of his severity toward them. This is the context of the hadith. There is no sense in taking it literally, so that we would go on to divide dutifulness between mother and father into thirds or quarters. This is what al-Qarafi questioned in a note in the twenty-third distinction (*al-Farq al-thalith wal-'ishrin*). For us, the wondrous arrangement of this verse on this matter is sufficient. As for the wording of the hadith, it is directed toward affirming dutifulness to the mother, out of fear of neglecting it. The meaning of "then" (*thumma*) in it is nothing but an echo of the questioner's words "then who?", as indicated by the fact that he joined the word "mother" with it in the two instances. There is no sense in preferring the mother over herself in dutifulness. Since the context is directed toward emphasis, it is determined that the conjunction of the father with the mother in the third instance is a conjunction in emphasis, and so no preponderance may be derived from it in case of conflict. Perhaps the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, understood from the questioner that he intended a permission for himself not to be dutiful. Malik was asked by a man: his father in the land of the Sudan had written to him to come to him, and his mother had forbidden him. Malik said to him: "Obey your father and do not disobey your mother." This indicates that he turned away from preferring one of the two parents, and that he held back in this conflict, so as to lead the son to please both of them. Al-Layth said: "The side of the mother is preferred." Al-Shafi'i said: "The side of the father is preferred."

The clause ﴿and his weaning is in two years﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿his mother bore him﴾ and so on, and it is likewise in the position of a circumstantial clause. In the clause there is an implied resumptive pronoun linking it to its subject, for the sense is: "and her weaning of him," and so when the weaning is attributed to its object, it is known that its agent is the mother.

*Al-fiṣāl* is a noun for weaning, that is, separation from nursing. It was mentioned earlier in His saying ﴿But if they both desire weaning﴾ [al-Baqarah: 233] in Surat al-Baqarah. The weaning is mentioned in the context of explaining the mother's greater entitlement to dutifulness, because it implies nursing before weaning, and to allude to what the mother bears of the distress of tenderness toward the nursling at the time of weaning, and what she witnesses of his sorrow and pain at the beginning of his weaning.

The longest period of his weaning is mentioned, which is two years, because that is most fitting for tenderness toward the mother. It is indicated that weaning may occur before two years by the use of the adverb of time *fi* (in), because the sense of inclusion in a container is satisfied when the contained fills the whole of the container. Therefore the position of *fi* is more eloquent than the position of *min* (partitive "from") in the verse of Sabra ibn 'Amr al-Faq'asi:

*Wa nashrabu fi athmanihā wa nuqāmiru*
And we drink in its price, and we gamble.

For it is satisfied when the drinking and the gambling consume the whole price of his camels. This was mentioned earlier at His saying ﴿and provide for them therein and clothe them﴾ [al-Nisa': 5] in Surat al-Nisa'. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib or Ibn 'Abbas was said to have interpreted it in this sense, and from it was derived that the minimum period of pregnancy is six months, by combining this verse with the verse of Surat al-Ahqaf, as will come there.

The clause ﴿Give thanks to Me and to your parents﴾ is an explanation of the verb *wassayna* (We enjoined). The *an* is explanatory (*tafsiriyyah*), and the command concerning parents was explained by what contains the command to thank God together with thanking them, by way of incorporation, as a preparation for His saying ﴿But if they strive with you to make you associate with Me﴾, and so on.

The clause ﴿To Me is the final return﴾ is a fresh beginning, for admonition and warning against opposing what God has enjoined, which is thanking Him. The definition of *al-maṣīr* (the final return) is a definition of genus, meaning the return of all people. You may also take *al* as a substitute for the genitive complement. The fronting of the prepositional phrase is for restriction, meaning: the idols have no return in intercession or anything else.

The discussion of the parallel of His saying ﴿And if they strive with you to make you associate with Me [al-'Ankabut: 8] up to ﴿do not obey them﴾ has been given in Surat al-'Ankabut, except that here He said ﴿on condition that you associate with Me﴾ (*'ala an tushrika bī*), and there in Surat al-'Ankabut He said ﴿to make you associate with Me﴾ (*li-tushrika bī*) [al-'Ankabut: 8]. As for the particle *'ala*, it is more indicative of the firmness of the striving, that is, a strong striving toward shirk. *Mujāhadah* (striving) is the intensity of effort and insistence. The meaning is: if they press and insist in calling you to associate partners with Me, then do not obey them. This is an emphasis on the prohibition against listening to them when they call to shirk.

As for the verse of al-'Ankabut, the particle of cause *li-* was used in it, to make clear that Sa'd was independent of emphasis on the prohibition against obeying his mother, because of the strength of his faith.

Al-Qurtubi said: "The wife of Luqman and his son were polytheists, and Luqman did not cease admonishing them until they believed." With this, the mention of the parents' striving to make their child associate partners with God becomes clearer.

*Al-muṣāḥabah* (keeping company) is living together in good fellowship. From it is the hadith of Mu'awiya ibn Haydah, that he said to the Messenger of God ﷺ: "Who is most deserving of the goodness of my companionship?" He said: "Your mother," and so on.

**Al-Ma'ruf** (what is known and customary, and therefore not objectionable) is what is good. The meaning is: keep company with your two parents in a good manner. *Ma'ruf* is in the accusative because it is an adjective of a verbal noun (*maṣdar*) that has been omitted, serving as an absolute object (*mafʿūl muṭlaq*) of *ṣāhibhumā* ("keep company with them"). The sense is: keep company with them in the manner of good companionship that is recognized among people like them.

From this is understood the avoidance of what is objectionable in their companionship. This includes the son treating his parents wrongly, and it includes a parent calling to what God disapproves of and does not accept. For this reason, they are not to be obeyed if they command disobedience.

From the mention of ﴿And keep company with them in this world with kindness﴾ following the clause ﴿But if they strive to make you associate with Me...﴾ and so on, it is understood that the command to live with them in kindness applies even when the parents are polytheists. The son must treat them with kindness, such as by doing good to them and maintaining ties with them.

In a hadith: "Asma' bint Abi Bakr said to the Messenger of God (ﷺ): 'My mother has come to me, desiring [my kindness]. Should I maintain ties with her?' He said: 'Yes, maintain ties with your mother.'" She was a polytheist, and she was Qutaylah bint ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā.

The term *al-maʿrūf* also includes what is recognized as permissible for them to do for themselves, even if it is objectionable for a Muslim. For this reason our jurists said: if a son spends on his poor disbelieving parents, and their habit is drinking wine, he may buy them wine, because drinking wine is not objectionable for a disbeliever. But if an act is objectionable in both religions, it is not permitted for a Muslim to assist either of his parents in it.

If we take the view that Luqman was not a prophet who conveyed a message from God, but a wise man who gave guidance, then this statement is a parenthetical insertion (*i'tiraḍ*, a phrase placed between parts of a discourse) between the two statements of Luqman. The form of this statement is cast in the style of conveying a message and of quoting one of God's sayings. The pronouns are pronouns of majesty. The context of Luqman's prohibition of his son from associating partners with God, and the description of that act as grave, brought this about. God thus mentioned this to reinforce what is in Luqman's counsel of prohibition against shirk, generalizing the prohibition to persons and circumstances, lest someone suppose that the prohibition applies only to Luqman's son or only to certain situations. God related that He had enjoined this on every human being, and that there is no leniency in it, even in the most difficult circumstances, which is the situation of parents striving to make their children associate partners with God.

A better explanation of the connection is this: when He related Luqman's counsel to his son, which was the thanks due to God by declaring Him free of association in divinity, God showed that He, may He be exalted, has the greater claim to bounty over His servants, in that He enjoined sons to be dutiful to their fathers. Thus the bounty upon Luqman was included in the general sense, as a reward for his observance of God's right at the outset of his admonition to his son. So God is more precedent in beneficence toward those who did good by observing His right. This interpretation is strengthened by the linking of thanks to God with thanks to the parents in the command.

If we take the view that Luqman was a prophet, then this statement is among what Luqman conveyed to his son, and it is among what he was given of revelation. It would have been related in the manner in which it was revealed to him, similar to the style of His saying ﴿Give thanks to God﴾ [Luqman: 12]. This possibility is more fitting to the context of the discourse, and it is preferred by the difference in style between it and the two verses of Surat al-'Ankabut and Surat al-Ahqaf, because what is here is a narration of what preceded in another community, whereas the other two are a fresh address to this community. It has been reported that when Luqman conveyed this to his son, he said to him: "God has been pleased with me for you, so He did not enjoin you upon me; and He was not pleased with you for me, so He enjoined you upon me."

The purpose of this statement is His saying ﴿But if they strive with you to make you associate with Me﴾ to the end of the verse, and what precedes it is a preparation for it and an establishment of the obligation of kindness to parents, so that the prohibition against obeying them becomes, in effect, a command to associate partners with God, a prohibition against it in the circumstance most deserving of obedience. Thus the prohibition against shirk in lesser circumstances is understood by implication of the discourse (*fahwa al-khiṭab*), together with the fine incorporation (*idmaj*) fitting to Luqman's wisdom, whether this is from Luqman's words or from God's, may He be exalted.

On both interpretations, what some exegetes have held is not good: that this verse was revealed concerning the case of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas's conversion to Islam and his mother's displeasure. This is because it does not fit the context, and because it has already been mentioned that the parallel of this verse in Surat al-'Ankabut was revealed about that. And it is that verse which is appropriate to the occasion of revelation, for it is free of the descriptions in which there is tenderness toward the mother, unlike this one. There is no basis for two verses to be revealed on a single purpose at different times. The one enjoined will be explained later.

*Al-wahn* (weakness), with the *ha'* vowelless, is the verbal noun of *wahana*, *yahinu*, from the pattern of *ḍaraba*. It is said also *wahan*, with the *ha'* vocalized, as the verbal noun of *wahana*, *yuhinu*, like *wajila*, *yawjalu*. It means weakness and lack of strength to bear something.

*Wahnan* is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) of *ummuhu* (his mother), for emphasis on her weakness, to the point that she is as if she were weakness itself, i.e., being weak in carrying him. *'Ala wahnin* is an attribute of *wahnan*, i.e., a weakness befalling upon weakness, as one says *raja'a 'awdan 'ala bad'in* ("he returned repeatedly to the beginning"), when one resumes a task he had finished and returns to it, i.e., after a beginning. Or *'ala* has the sense of *ma'a* (with), as in the verse of al-Ahwas:

*Inni 'ala ma qad 'alimta muḥassadun*
*anmi 'ala al-baghḍa'i wal-shana'ani*

Indeed, despite what you know, I am envied;
I grow up amid hatred and enmity.

The pregnancy of a woman is accompanied by fatigue from the weight of the fetus in the womb, and by weakness from the diversion of her blood to nourishing the fetus. That weakness continues to increase as the period of pregnancy lengthens. Therefore it is undoubtedly a weakness upon weakness.

The clause ﴿his mother bore him in weakness upon weakness﴾ is in the position of a reason (ta'lil) for the command concerning parents, intended to reinforce that command, because the stating of the reason for a ruling affirms it, and because the content of this clause stirs in the child's soul the motive to be dutiful to his mother, and this leads to dutifulness to his father too.

The reason for the command concerning the parents was stated by mentioning circumstances specific to one of them, namely the mother, relying on the fact that this condition requires the command concerning the father too, by analogy (*qiyas*). The father encounters hardships and fatigue in providing for the mother, so that she may be free to attend to the child during the period of his care. Then he takes charge of his upbringing and protection until he reaches his maturity and no longer needs support, as God, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And say: My Lord, have mercy on them both as they raised me when I was small﴾ [al-Isra': 24]. Thus He combined them in raising the child in his infancy, which concerns his preservation and the completion of his upbringing. So when the condition that requires dutifulness to the mother is mentioned here, namely carrying and nursing, it serves as an alert to the condition of the father that requires dutifulness to him, in proportion to what the same cause requires in both, in strength and weakness. The difference in the strength of the quality that justifies the extension of the ruling does not invalidate the analogy between the analogue and its base. This analogy is indicated by the joining of the two in the command to be grateful, immediately after it, in His saying ﴿Give thanks to Me and to your parents﴾ and His saying ﴿and keep them company in this world with kindness﴾.

From this wondrous arrangement is achieved the fulfilment of the right of conciseness (*ījāz*).

As for the preponderance of the mother in this matter when the demands of dutifulness conflict in a way in which reconciliation is not possible, Ibn 'Atiyyah said in his exegesis: "God, in this verse, placed the mother and the father in the same rank of the command concerning them, then singled out the mother by mention of the stage of carrying and the stage of nursing, so that the mother has three degrees and the father one. This resembles the saying of the Messenger ﷺ when a man said to him: 'Who is most deserving of my good companionship?' He said: 'Your mother.' He said: 'Then who?' He said: 'Your mother.' He said: 'Then who?' He said: 'Your mother.' He said: 'Then who?' He said: 'Your father.' So he was given a quarter of the dutifulness." This statement, similar to it, is attributed to Ibn Battal in his commentary on Sahih al-Bukhari.

It is not hidden that the context of the hadith is to affirm dutifulness to the mother, since failing in the due obligation to the mother may occur on the part of the son, relying on the gentleness he receives from her, unlike the case of the father, who is strong, and whose children are wary of his severity toward them. This is the context of the hadith. There is no sense in taking it literally, so that we would go on to divide dutifulness between mother and father into thirds or quarters. This is what al-Qarafi questioned in a note in the twenty-third distinction (*al-Farq al-thalith wal-'ishrin*). For us, the wondrous arrangement of this verse on this matter is sufficient. As for the wording of the hadith, it is directed toward affirming dutifulness to the mother, out of fear of neglecting it. The meaning of "then" (*thumma*) in it is nothing but an echo of the questioner's words "then who?", as indicated by the fact that he joined the word "mother" with it in the two instances. There is no sense in preferring the mother over herself in dutifulness. Since the context is directed toward emphasis, it is determined that the conjunction of the father with the mother in the third instance is a conjunction in emphasis, and so no preponderance may be derived from it in case of conflict. Perhaps the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, understood from the questioner that he intended a permission for himself not to be dutiful. Malik was asked by a man: his father in the land of the Sudan had written to him to come to him, and his mother had forbidden him. Malik said to him: "Obey your father and do not disobey your mother." This indicates that he turned away from preferring one of the two parents, and that he held back in this conflict, so as to lead the son to please both of them. Al-Layth said: "The side of the mother is preferred." Al-Shafi'i said: "The side of the father is preferred."

The clause ﴿and his weaning is in two years﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿his mother bore him﴾ and so on, and it is likewise in the position of a circumstantial clause. In the clause there is an implied resumptive pronoun linking it to its subject, for the sense is: "and her weaning of him," and so when the weaning is attributed to its object, it is known that its agent is the mother.

*Al-fiṣāl* is a noun for weaning, that is, separation from nursing. It was mentioned earlier in His saying ﴿But if they both desire weaning﴾ [al-Baqarah: 233] in Surat al-Baqarah. The weaning is mentioned in the context of explaining the mother's greater entitlement to dutifulness, because it implies nursing before weaning, and to allude to what the mother bears of the distress of tenderness toward the nursling at the time of weaning, and what she witnesses of his sorrow and pain at the beginning of his weaning.

The longest period of his weaning is mentioned, which is two years, because that is most fitting for tenderness toward the mother. It is indicated that weaning may occur before two years by the use of the adverb of time *fi* (in), because the sense of inclusion in a container is satisfied when the contained fills the whole of the container. Therefore the position of *fi* is more eloquent than the position of *min* (partitive "from") in the verse of Sabra ibn 'Amr al-Faq'asi:

*Wa nashrabu fi athmanihā wa nuqāmiru*
And we drink in its price, and we gamble.

For it is satisfied when the drinking and the gambling consume the whole price of his camels. This was mentioned earlier at His saying ﴿and provide for them therein and clothe them﴾ [al-Nisa': 5] in Surat al-Nisa'. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib or Ibn 'Abbas was said to have interpreted it in this sense, and from it was derived that the minimum period of pregnancy is six months, by combining this verse with the verse of Surat al-Ahqaf, as will come there.

The clause ﴿Give thanks to Me and to your parents﴾ is an explanation of the verb *wassayna* (We enjoined). The *an* is explanatory (*tafsiriyyah*), and the command concerning parents was explained by what contains the command to thank God together with thanking them, by way of incorporation, as a preparation for His saying ﴿But if they strive with you to make you associate with Me﴾, and so on.

The clause ﴿To Me is the final return﴾ is a fresh beginning, for admonition and warning against opposing what God has enjoined, which is thanking Him. The definition of *al-maṣīr* (the final return) is a definition of genus, meaning the return of all people. You may also take *al* as a substitute for the genitive complement. The fronting of the prepositional phrase is for restriction, meaning: the idols have no return in intercession or anything else.

The discussion of the parallel of His saying ﴿And if they strive with you to make you associate with Me [al-'Ankabut: 8] up to ﴿do not obey them﴾ has been given in Surat al-'Ankabut, except that here He said ﴿on condition that you associate with Me﴾ (*'ala an tushrika bī*), and there in Surat al-'Ankabut He said ﴿to make you associate with Me﴾ (*li-tushrika bī*) [al-'Ankabut: 8]. As for the particle *'ala*, it is more indicative of the firmness of the striving, that is, a strong striving toward shirk. *Mujāhadah* (striving) is the intensity of effort and insistence. The meaning is: if they press and insist in calling you to associate partners with Me, then do not obey them. This is an emphasis on the prohibition against listening to them when they call to shirk.

As for the verse of al-'Ankabut, the particle of cause *li-* was used in it, to make clear that Sa'd was independent of emphasis on the prohibition against obeying his mother, because of the strength of his faith.

Al-Qurtubi said: "The wife of Luqman and his son were polytheists, and Luqman did not cease admonishing them until they believed." With this, the mention of the parents' striving to make their child associate partners with God becomes clearer.

*Al-muṣāḥabah* (keeping company) is living together in good fellowship. From it is the hadith of Mu'awiya ibn Haydah, that he said to the Messenger of God ﷺ: "Who is most deserving of the goodness of my companionship?" He said: "Your mother," and so on.

**Al-Ma'ruf** (what is known and customary, and therefore not objectionable) is what is good. The meaning is: keep company with your two parents in a good manner. *Ma'ruf* is in the accusative because it is an adjective of a verbal noun (*maṣdar*) that has been omitted, serving as an absolute object (*mafʿūl muṭlaq*) of *ṣāhibhumā* ("keep company with them"). The sense is: keep company with them in the manner of good companionship that is recognized among people like them.

From this is understood the avoidance of what is objectionable in their companionship. This includes the son treating his parents wrongly, and it includes a parent calling to what God disapproves of and does not accept. For this reason, they are not to be obeyed if they command disobedience.

From the mention of ﴿And keep company with them in this world with kindness﴾ following the clause ﴿But if they strive to make you associate with Me...﴾ and so on, it is understood that the command to live with them in kindness applies even when the parents are polytheists. The son must treat them with kindness, such as by doing good to them and maintaining ties with them.

In a hadith: "Asma' bint Abi Bakr said to the Messenger of God (ﷺ): 'My mother has come to me, desiring [my kindness]. Should I maintain ties with her?' He said: 'Yes, maintain ties with your mother.'" She was a polytheist, and she was Qutaylah bint ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā.
