Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 31, verse 16:

﴿O my son, indeed it, if it be the weight of a mustard seed, and it be within a rock or in the heavens or in the earth, Allah will bring it forth. Indeed, Allah is Subtle, Acquainted.﴾

The repetition of the call (nida') serves to renew the listener's attention so that he comprehends the speech.

Nafi' and Abu Ja'far read ﴿إنْ تَكُ مِثْقالُ﴾ with the nominative (raf') on (mithqal), taking it as the subject (fa'il) of (taku) from (kana) in its complete sense (al-tammah). The feminine ta' of the present tense was used with its verb because (mithqal) is grammatically masculine, but it was attached to the feminine (habbah) through idafah, so it acquired the feminine gender from the genitive noun. This is a common usage when the annexed noun, if omitted, would not disrupt the sentence such that the annexed noun (mudaf ilayh) can stand in for the annexing noun (mudaf). Accordingly, the pronoun in ﴿إنَّها﴾ refers to the matter and the event, and it is what is called the pronoun of the matter (damir al-sha'n). It takes the form of the feminine singular pronoun by way of interpreting it as "the matter." The feminine form of this pronoun is preferred when the story contains a feminine noun, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿فَإنَّها لا تَعْمى الأبْصارُ﴾ [al-Hajj: 46]. The pronoun of the matter frequently occurs after (inna), as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿إنَّهُ مَن يَأْتِ رَبَّهُ مُجْرِمًا فَإنَّ لَهُ جَهَنَّمَ لا يَمُوتُ فِيها ولا يَحْيا﴾ [Ta-Ha: 74]. Among this is the estimation of the pronoun of the matter as the noun of the light (harf) (anna), which is opened and lightened, and it conveys emphasis on the addressee's attentiveness to what follows. Thus three emphatic devices are gathered in this sentence: the call, (inna), and the pronoun of the matter, on account of the great significance of what follows, which establishes His description, exalted is He, with knowledge encompassing all known things among existents, and His description with power encompassing all possible things, as indicated by His saying ﴿يَأْتِ بِها اللَّهُ﴾.

This has been conveyed by way of the indication of the stronger meaning (dalalat al-fahwa): the most minute of existents in terms of the relation of knowledge and power to it is mentioned, namely the finest of bodies, concealed in the hardest place or its farthest and most inaccessible, or its widest and most widely dispersed, so that it may be known that what is greater than it in manifestness and nearness to reach is more deserving of being encompassed by Allah's knowledge and power.

The rest read (mithqal) with the accusative (nasb) as the predicate (khabar) of (taku) from (kana) in its incomplete sense (al-naqisah), with an implied subject for it that the context indicates, while the verb is attributed to a feminine noun. That is, "if there exists" the thing (al-ka'inah): the pronoun of ﴿إنَّها﴾ intends the trait, whether good or evil, taken from the context.

Al-mithqal, with a kasra on the mim, is that by which weight is measured, and for this reason it is formed on the pattern of the instrument noun.

Al-habbah is the singular of al-habb, which is the seed of plants, of grains or legumes, such that that single unit is a seed for its kind of plant. The saying of His, exalted is He, ﴿كَمَثَلِ حَبَّةٍ أنْبَتَتْ سَبْعَ سَنابِلَ﴾ [al-Baqarah: 261], and His saying ﴿إنَّ اللَّهَ فالِقُ الحَبِّ والنَّوى﴾ [al-An'am: 95] in Surat al-An'am, have already preceded.

Al-khardal (mustard) is a plant with a root and an upright, branching, cylindrical stem, with large leaves, which produces small yellow spike-like flowers that turn into fine, square-angled pods that yield fine seeds also called khardal. The core of these seeds is very hot, stinging the tongue and skin. They burst open easily, their husk splitting by pounding or when moistened with a liquid, so they are used in medicines as poultices on places where there is internal inflammation from a catarrh or pleurisy. It is very commonly used in medicine, past and present, though physicians have begun to dispense with it in favour of other drugs. A parallel to this has preceded in Surat al-Anbiya', ﴿فَلا تُظْلَمُ نَفْسٌ شَيْئًا وإنْ كانَ مِثْقالَ حَبَّةٍ مِن خَرْدَلٍ أتَيْنا بِها﴾ [al-Anbiya': 47].

His saying ﴿أوْ في السَّماواتِ﴾ is conjoined to ﴿فِي صَخْرَةٍ﴾, because the rock is part of the earth; so after it He mentioned ﴿أوْ في السَّماواتِ﴾, meaning "or [it be] in the heavens, which are more inaccessible than the rock," and He conjoined to it ﴿أوْ في الأرْضِ﴾, though the rock is a part of the earth, for the purpose of generalizing earthly places, since the sense of location (zarfiyyah) is true of both. That is, all of this is equal with respect to the scope of Allah's knowledge and power, as if He had said: "it be in a rock, or wherever it may be, of the upper world and the lower world." This is the meaning of His saying ﴿وما يَعْزُبُ عَنْ رَبِّكَ مِن مِثْقالِ ذَرَّةٍ في الأرْضِ ولا في السَّماءِ ولا أصْغَرَ مِن ذَلِكَ ولا أكْبَرَ إلّا في كِتابٍ مُبِينٍ﴾ [Yunus: 61].

The bringing (al-ityan) is a metonymy for the capacity to act upon it, and it is also a symbolic metonymy for knowledge of it, because bringing the finest of bodies from the farthest, deepest and hardest places is not possible except through knowledge that it is in that place and knowledge of the means of extracting it from there.

The clause ﴿إنَّ اللَّهَ لَطِيفٌ خَبِيرٌ﴾ may be from the speech of Luqman, in which case it serves as the purpose of the premise or as the conclusion of the proof, and for this reason it is detached (fusilat) and not conjoined, because the conclusion is like a substitute of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal), which the syllogism comprises; therefore the conclusion was brought universal after the argument from a particular. We have not made it a cause (ta'lil), because the context of Luqman teaching his son requires that the son is ignorant of these realities, and the condition of a cause is that it be an accepted and known matter prior to knowledge of the caused thing, so that the reasoning from it is valid.
It may also be a parenthetical insertion (mu'taridah) between the words of Luqman, as an instruction from Allah to the Muslims.

Al-Latif is one who knows the subtleties of things and, in bringing them to those fit for them, follows the path of gentleness. It is therefore a description that indicates complete knowledge and power: that is, He knows, determines and executes His power. It has preceded in His saying ﴿وهُوَ اللَّطِيفُ الخَبِيرُ﴾ [al-An'am: 103] in Surat al-An'am.

Thus, in following ﴿يَأْتِ بِها اللَّهُ﴾ with the description "al-Latif" there is an allusion that the capacity over it and its possession occurs in a subtle manner suited to splitting the rock and extracting the mustard seed from it while keeping both it and what is connected to them intact, without disruption of the order of His creation. Here He has completed the foundations of correct belief.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 31, verse 17:

﴿O my son, establish the prayer, enjoin what is right, forbid what is wrong, and bear patiently whatever befalls you. Indeed, that is of the determined matters.﴾

He moved from teaching him the foundations of belief (usul al-'aqidah) to teaching him the foundations of righteous deeds, beginning with the establishment of the prayer (iqamat al-salah). The prayer is turning toward God in humility, glorification and supplication at specified times in the sacred law (al-shari'ah) that Luqman adhered to. The prayer is the pillar (imad) of deeds, because it includes acknowledgment of obedience to God and a request for guidance to righteous action.

Establishing the prayer (iqamat al-salah) means perpetuating it and being diligent in performing it at its appointed times. This was discussed at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah.

The command to enjoin what is right (al-amr bi'l-ma'ruf) encompasses performing all righteous deeds in general terms, so that their details are sought within the admonitions of his father. Likewise, the prohibition of what is wrong (al-nahy 'an al-munkar) encompasses abstaining from evil deeds.

The command that he enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong requires that the command and its prohibition be first applied to himself, because the one who enjoins good and forbids evil knows what good and evil deeds contain, of benefits (masalih) and harms (mafasid). Therefore it is inevitable that he should guard himself against them, with priority over his commanding people and forbidding them.

This is thus a comprehensive statement of wisdom (hikmah) and piety (taqwa), for he combined for his son guidance to doing good and spreading it among people, restraining himself from evil and deterring people from committing it. Then he followed this by commanding him to be patient over what afflicts him.

The reason for linking the command to enjoin right and forbid wrong with the constant practice of patience is that enjoining right and forbidding wrong may bring upon the one who performs them hostility from some people or harm from others. If he does not patiently bear what befalls him as a consequence of enjoining right and forbidding wrong, he is likely to abandon them.

Since the benefit of patience returns to the one who is patient, through a great reward, patience is counted here among the deeds whose benefit is confined to their doer, and it does not refer to what there is in enduring people's harm of good dealing with them, to the point of mentioning patience alongside His saying (and do not turn your cheek away from people). This is because that is not the primary intent of the command to be patient.

Patience (al-sabr) is enduring what befalls a person of that which causes pain or grief. It was discussed earlier in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And seek help through patience and prayer﴾ [al-Baqarah: 45], in Surat al-Baqarah.

The clause ﴿Indeed, that is of the determined matters﴾ holds the same position as the clause ﴿Indeed, associating others with God is a great injustice﴾ [Luqman: 13].

The clause ﴿Indeed, God is Subtle, All-Aware﴾ [Luqman: 16] may be part of Luqman's speech, or it may be a parenthetical statement from God, exalted is He.

The demonstrative "that" (dhalika) refers to what was mentioned: establishing the prayer, enjoining right, forbidding wrong, and patience over what befalls. The emphasis (al-ta'kid) is for the sake of attention and importance.

Al-'azm is a verbal noun meaning decisiveness (al-jazm) and obligation (al-ilzam). The 'azimah is the resolve in which there is no hesitation.

And "'azm" is a verbal noun used in the sense of the passive participle, i.e., from the determined matters (ma'zum al-umur), that is, those which God has determined and made obligatory.

Commentary of Ibn ʿAshur (al-Taḥrīr wa al-Tanwīr) on Surah 31, verse 18:

﴿And do not turn your cheek away from people in contempt, nor walk on the earth exultantly. Indeed, Allah does not love every arrogant boaster.﴾

Luqman moved on to his son's manners in dealing with people, so he forbade him from despising people and from boasting over them. This requires him to show his equality with people and to count himself as one of them.

The majority of readers recited (ولا تُصاعِرْ) (*wa-lā tuṣāʿir*). Ibn Kathīr, Ibn ʿĀmir, ʿĀṣim, Abū Jaʿfar and Yaʿqūb recited (ولا تُصَعِّرْ) (*wa-lā tuṣaʿʿir*). It is said: *ṣāʿara* and *ṣaʿʿara* mean that he inclined his neck to one side in order to turn away from the other side. It is derived from *al-ṣaʿar* (a condition of the camel's neck), with a vowel on the first letter, a disease that afflicts the camel so that it twists its neck from it. The verb was therefore given a form of effort, with the meaning of effortfully displaying *ṣaʿar*. This is a figurative image (*tamthīl*) for contempt, because turning the cheek away is the posture of one who despises and belittles, in most cases.

ʿAmr ibn Ḥunayy al-Taghlibī said, addressing one of their kings:

*And when a tyrant turned his cheek aside, we straightened him from his inclination, and he became upright.*

The meaning is: do not hold people in contempt. The prohibition on turning away from them out of contempt is not specifically about turning the cheek, so it includes contempt expressed through speech, insults and other means. It is close to His saying ﴿So do not say to them, "Uff"﴾ (Al-Isrāʾ: 23), except that this is a figurative metaphor (*tamthīl kināʾī*), whereas the other is a metonymy (*kināya*) with no figurative image in it.

Likewise His saying ﴿nor walk on the earth exultantly﴾ is a figurative metaphor (*tamthīl kināʾī*) for the prohibition of arrogance. It is not specifically about walking in a state of exultation, so it includes boasting over people through speech and other means.

[Page 167]

*Al-maraḥ* (exultation) is an excess of energy arising from joy and self-admiration, and this appears in walking as strutting and swaggering. For this reason that walk is called *maraḥ*, as in the verse. Its position is as an attribute of an absolute object (*al-mafʿūl al-muṭlaq*, the cognate accusative), meaning *mashyan maraḥan* (a walk in exultation). This was discussed in Surah al-Isrāʾ. The placement of *fī al-arḍ* ("on the earth") after *lā tamshi* ("do not walk"), even though walking can only be on the earth, indicates that walking should take place in a place where all people walk, strong and weak alike. In this there is an admonition to the one who walks exultantly, that he is equal to the rest of humanity.

The placement of ﴿Indeed, Allah does not love every arrogant boaster﴾ corresponds to ﴿Indeed, Allah is Subtle, Aware﴾ (Luqmān: 16), as previously mentioned. *Al-mukhtāl* is an active participle from *ikhtāla*, in the pattern *iftaʿala*, from the verb *khāla*, when someone is possessed of *khuyalāʾ* (self-conceit), so he is *khāʾil*. *Al-khuyalāʾ* is pride and self-admiration. The *iftiʿāl* form here is for intensification in the description, so the pattern of *al-mukhtāl* is *mukhtiyil*. When the weak letter moved and the letter before it was opened, it was changed to an *alif*. Thus His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah does not love every arrogant boaster﴾ corresponds to His saying "and do not turn your cheek away from people", and His saying (*fakhūran*, "boastful") corresponds to His saying ﴿nor walk on the earth exultantly﴾.

*Al-fakhūr* means one who boasts excessively. It was discussed in His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah does not love whoever is arrogant and boastful﴾ (Al-Nisāʾ: 36) in Surah al-Nisāʾ.

The meaning of ﴿Indeed, Allah does not love every arrogant boaster﴾ is that Allah is not pleased with any of the arrogant, boastful people. It does not occur to people of linguistic practice that its implication is that Allah does not love the collective of arrogant, boastful people when they gather together, based on what ʿAbd al-Qāhir mentioned: that when *kull* ("every") is placed within the scope of negation and comes after its particle, the negation falls on totality. This is true only of *kull* when it is intended to emphasize comprehensiveness, not of *kull* when it is intended to refer to individuals, and the decision in such cases depends on contextual indicators. Moreover, we see that what the Shaykh mentioned is a general tendency, not a consistent rule in the usage of the people of the language. For this reason we find the correctness of both the nominative and accusative readings of the word *kull* in the verse of Abū al-Najm al-ʿIjlī:

*Umm al-Khiyār has begun to claim against me a wrong, all of which I did not commit.*

I have explained this in my glosses on *Dalāʾil al-Iʿjāz*.

[Page 168]

The position of the clause ﴿Indeed, Allah does not love every arrogant boaster﴾ admits of what has passed for the clause ﴿Indeed, shirk is a tremendous wrong﴾ (Luqmān: 13), the clause ﴿Indeed, Allah is Subtle, Aware﴾ (Luqmān: 16), and the clause ﴿Indeed, that is of the determined matters﴾ (Luqmān: 17).

**[Page 169]**

Ibn 'Ashur, *al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir*, on Surah 31, verse 19:

﴿And be moderate in your walking and lower your voice. Indeed, the most disagreeable of voices is the voice of donkeys.﴾

After (the verse) had set out for him the etiquette of good conduct with people, it followed it with good etiquette in his personal condition, namely the two states of walking and speaking, which are the most visible things that show a person's manners.

*Al-qasd* (moderation) means the middle course that is just between two extremes. Moderation in walking is to be between the extreme of strutting (*al-tabakhtur*) and the extreme of dragging along (*al-dabib*). It is said: "He was moderate in his walking" (*qasada fi mashyihi*). So the meaning of ﴿be moderate in your walking﴾ is: adopt moderation.

*Al-ghadd* (lowering) is the reduction of the strength with which a thing is used. It is said: "He lowered his gaze" (*ghadda basarahu*) when he lowered his look and did not stare. The words of God Most High, ﴿Tell the believing men to lower their gaze﴾ [al-Nur: 30], were mentioned earlier in Surah al-Nur. Thus *ghadd al-sawt* (lowering the voice) means making it less than loud.

The particle *min* (some of), which indicates partiality, is used to convey that he lowers part of it, that is, part of his loudness. He reduces its volume, but he does not go so far as to whisper or speak in secret.

The clause ﴿indeed, the most disagreeable of voices is the voice of donkeys﴾ is a justification (*ta'lil*) given for the command to lower one's voice. It is taken as containing an eloquent simile (*tashbih baligh*), meaning: because the voice of donkeys is the most disagreeable of voices. Raising the voice in speech resembles the braying of donkeys, so it has a share of that disagreeableness.

*Ankar* is an elative (*ism tafdil*) in the sense of the voice being described as *munkar* (disagreeable). It is an elative derived from a verb in the passive voice. This form is attested (*sama'i*), not anomalous, and from it comes the proverb: "More preoccupied than the woman of the two jars" (*ashghal min dhat al-nahyayn*), meaning: more busy than the woman mentioned in this proverb.

As for why the Qur'an used the plural *al-hamir* (the donkeys) though *sawt* is singular, and did not say *al-himar*: the noun defined by the generic article (*lam al-jins*) has the same form in the singular and the plural. For this reason it is said that when the generic article enters a plural, it removes the sense of plurality from it. The plural form was preferred because the word *al-hamir* suits the verse-endings (*fawasil*). Among the merits of verse-endings and rhymed phrases (*asjac*) is that they follow the rules of rhyme (*qawafi*). A rhyme founded on a *waw* or a *ya'* (*al-qafiya al-mu'assasa*) may not be accompanied by an *alif* of foundation (*alif al-ta'sis*). The verse-endings preceding ﴿And We had certainly given Luqman wisdom﴾ [Luqman: 12] are: *hamid*, *azim*, *al-masir*, *khabir*, *al-umur*, *fakhur*, *al-hamir*. The verse-endings of the Qur'an depend largely on vowels, lengthenings and forms, not on the matching of letters, and in this way they differ from the rhymes of poems.

This fulfils what I promised when speaking about the words of God Most High, ﴿And We had certainly given Luqman wisdom﴾ [Luqman: 12], namely to mention the outcome of my search for what has been transmitted of the wisdom of Luqman beyond what is in this surah. Al-Alusi, in his tafsir, mentioned twenty-eight of them, which are:

His saying to his son: "O my son, indeed the world is a deep sea, and many people have drowned in it. So make your ship in it the fear of God Most High, let its hull be faith, and its sail reliance upon God Most High, perhaps you will be saved, but I do not see you as one who is saved."

His saying: "Whoever has a preacher within himself, God, Mighty and Majestic, will have a guardian for him. Whoever is just to people with regard to himself, God Most High will increase him in honour thereby. Humility in obedience to God Most High is closer than seeking honour through disobedience."

His saying: "A father's beating of his son is like manure for the crop."

His saying: "O my son, beware of debt, for it is humiliation by day and worry by night."

His saying: "O my son, hope in God, Mighty and Majestic, with a hope that does not lead you to disobey Him, and fear God, Glorified be He, with a fear that does not make you despair of His mercy, exalted be His station."

His saying: "Whoever lies loses the brightness of his face, whoever has bad character, his sorrow multiplies, and moving rocks from their places is easier than making understood one who does not understand."

His saying: "O my son, I have carried stones, iron and every heavy thing, but I have not carried anything heavier than a bad neighbour. I have tasted bitterness, but I have not tasted anything more bitter than poverty."

"O my son, do not send your messenger ignorant. If you do not find a wise man, then be your own messenger."

"O my son, beware of lying, for it is as tempting as the flesh of a sparrow, and before long its practitioner will be boiled."

"O my son, attend funerals and do not attend weddings, for funerals remind you of the Hereafter, while weddings make you desire this world."

"O my son, do not eat to satiety upon satiety, for throwing it to the dog is better than your eating it."

"O my son, do not be sweet lest you be swallowed, and do not be bitter lest you be spat out."

His saying: "Let none eat your food except the pious, and consult the scholars in your affairs."

His saying: "There is no good for you in learning what you do not know while you do not act upon what you already know. The likeness of that is the likeness of a man who gathered firewood, took up a bundle and went off carrying it, but became unable to bear it, so he added another to it."

His saying: "O my son, when you want to befriend a man, first anger him. If he is just with you when angry, (then befriend him), otherwise beware of him."

His saying: "Let your word be good and your face cheerful, and you will be more beloved to people than one who gives them gifts."

His saying: "O my son, place yourself in the position, with regard to your companion, of one who has no need of you but whom you cannot do without."

"O my son, be like one who does not seek people's praise nor earn their blame. His soul is in toil from it, while people are at ease from him."

His saying: "O my son, restrain what comes out of your mouth, for you are safe as long as you are silent, and you should only say what benefits you."

I now follow these with what al-Alusi did not mention.

Among them is what is in the *Muwatta'* of Malik, in what came concerning the seeking of knowledge, in the *Kitab al-Jami'*: Malik reported that it reached him that Luqman the Wise advised his son, saying: "O my son, sit with the scholars and press upon them with your knees, for God gives life to hearts with the light of knowledge, as He gives life to dead earth with the heavy rain of the sky."

And in it, in what came concerning truthfulness and lying in the *Kitab al-Jami'*: it reached him that it was said to Luqman: "What has reached you that we see? They seek superiority." He said: "Truthfulness of speech, fulfilling trusts, and leaving what does not concern me."

And in the *Jami' al-Mustakhraja* of al-Utbi, Malik said: "It reached me that Luqman said to his son: 'O my son, let the first thing you gain from this world, after a righteous friend, be a righteous wife.'"

And in *Ahkam al-Qur'an* of Ibn al-'Arabi, from Malik: that Luqman said to his son: "O my son, indeed people have been long subjected to what they are promised, while they hasten toward the Hereafter. You have turned your back on this world since you were (born) and faced the Hereafter, and indeed a house you are travelling toward is nearer to you than a house you are leaving." He also said: "No wealth is like health, and no blessing is like contentment of soul." He said: "O my son, do not sit with the wicked nor walk with them, lest a punishment descend upon them from heaven and strike you along with them." He said: "O my son, sit with the scholars and walk with them, perhaps a mercy will descend upon them and reach you along with them."

In al-Kashshaf: that he said to a man who was looking at him: "If you see me as thick-lipped, indeed there comes out from between them a delicate speech, and if you see me as black, my heart is white." And that his master ordered him to slaughter a sheep and bring him the two best pieces, so he brought him the tongue and the heart. Then he ordered him to slaughter another and to throw away the two worst pieces, so he threw away the tongue and the heart. (The master) asked him about that, and he said: "They are the best of what is in it when they are good, and the worst of what is in it when they are bad."

He entered upon David while he was weaving coats of mail, and he wanted to ask him what he was doing, but wisdom overtook him and he remained silent. When David finished it, he put it on and said: "How excellent a coat of war you are!" Luqman said: "Silence is wisdom, and few practise it."

In the tafsir of Ibn 'Atiyya: it was said to Luqman: "Which of people is the worst?" He said: "One who does not care whether people see him as bad or as doing bad."

In the tafsir of al-Qurtubi: Luqman used to give legal opinions (*yufti*) before the mission of David. When David was sent, he ceased giving legal opinions. It was said to him (about this), and he said: "Shall I not be content when I have been relieved (of the burden)?" And in it: indeed the judge is in the most difficult and troubled position, where the wronged come to him from every place. If he is right, he should hope to be saved, and if he errs, he errs on the path to Paradise. Whoever is humble in this world is better than whoever is noble (in it). Whoever prefers this world to the Hereafter, this world will escape him and he will not attain the Hereafter.

In the tafsir of al-Baydawi: that David asked Luqman: "How have you become?" He said: "I have become in the hand of another."

In *Durrat al-Tanzil*, attributed to Fakhr al-Din al-Razi: Luqman said to his son: "Indeed God has chosen me for you, so He did not entrust you to me, and He did not make you pleasing to me, so He entrusted you to me."

In *al-Shifa'* of 'Iyad: Luqman said to his son: "When the stomach is filled, thought sleeps, wisdom becomes mute, and the limbs sit idle from worship."

In the *Kitab Adab al-Nikah* of Qasim ibn Ya'mun al-Talidi al-Akhmasi: that among the counsels of Luqman was: "O my son, the likeness of a righteous woman is like the oil on the head: it softens the veins and beautifies the hair. Her likeness is like the crown on the head of a king, and her likeness is like pearls and jewels, of which no one knows the value."

"And the likeness of an evil woman is like a flood that does not stop until it reaches its end. When she speaks, she makes (all) hear; when she walks, she hastens; when she sits, she rises up; and when she is angry, she makes (all) hear. Every disease can be cured except the disease of an evil woman."

"O my son, to dwell with lions and lionesses is better for you than to dwell with a woman who weeps while she is the wrongdoer, judges while she is the oppressor, and speaks while she is the ignorant one, and she is a viper with its bite."

In *Majma' al-Bayan* of al-Tabarsi: "O my son, travel with your sword, your slippers, your turban, your tent, your waterskin, your thread and your awl, and take with you of medicines what benefits you and those with you. Be agreeable to your companions except in disobedience to God, Mighty and Majestic. O my son, when you travel with a people, ask their counsel much in your affairs and theirs, smile much in their faces, and be generous with your provisions among them. When they call you, answer them, and when they seek your help, help them. Make long silence and much prayer your habit, and be generous with your soul in (sharing) whatever you have of mount, water or provisions. When they call you to witness for the truth, bear witness for them. Exert your opinion for them when they consult you, but do not resolve (on anything) until you have considered and reflected. Do not give counsel on a matter until you have stood and sat in it, slept and eaten and prayed, while you are employing your thought and wisdom in its consultation, for whoever does not give sincere counsel to one who consults him, God will strip him of his judgment. When you see your companions walking, walk with them; when you see them working, work with them; and listen to one who is older than you in age. When they command you with a matter or ask you for something, say 'Yes' and do not say 'No,' for 'No' is weakness and baseness. When you lose your way on the road, dismount; when you doubt the direction, stop and consult together. When you see a single person, do not ask him about your road nor seek his guidance, for a single person in the wilderness is suspicious: perhaps he is a spy of the robbers, or he is the devil who has led you astray. Beware of two persons also, unless you see what I do not see, for the intelligent man, when he sees a thing with his own eyes, knows the truth of it, and the witness sees what the absent one does not see."

"O my son, when the time of prayer comes, do not delay it for anything. Pray it and be relieved of it, for it is a debt. Pray in congregation, even if it is at the top of a spear-point. When you wish to halt, choose from the land's places the best in colour, the softest in soil, and the most abundant in grass. When you halt, pray two rak'ahs before you sit down. When you want to relieve yourself, go far away into the earth. When you depart, pray two rak'ahs, then bid farewell to the land where you have stayed and greet its people, for every place has its inhabitants among the angels. If you can, do not eat any food until you begin by giving alms from it, then do so. Let it be your practice to recite the Book of God (perhaps he means the Psalms) while you are riding, to glorify God while you are working, and to supplicate while you are at leisure. Beware of travelling from the beginning of the night to its end, and beware of raising your voice while you journey."

Thus we have traced what we found of the wisdom of Luqman, which approaches seventy sayings.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 31, verses 20–21:

﴿Have you not seen that Allah has subjected to you whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and has completed His favours upon you, both outward and inward?﴾

This is a return to enumerating the proofs of God's oneness (tawhid) and the blessings that accompany them upon creation. The discourse is therefore a fresh, initiatory resumption (istinaf ibtida'i) from the preceding discourse, and a return to what preceded at the beginning of the surah,

in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿He created the heavens without pillars﴾ [Luqman: 10]. For after argument from the creation of the heavens, the earth, living beings and rain, the argument and the bestowal of favour return here: that He has subjected to us what is in the heavens and what is on the earth. The discussion of this subjection has already passed in the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Allah is the One who created the heavens and the earth﴾ [Ibrahim: 32], the verses of Surah Ibrahim, and likewise in Surah al-Nahl.

The meaning of (subjected to you) is "for your sake," because among that subjection are benefits for us: rain, winds, the light of the sun and moon, the timings of the constellations, the stations (manazil) of the moon, and orientation by them. The address in (Have you not seen) may be to all people, believers and polytheists alike, since it is a bestowal of favour; and it may be specific to the polytheists, given that it is an argument.

The interrogative in (Have you not seen) is for affirmation (taqrir) or denial (inkar) of the non-seeing, by treating them as those who have not seen the traces of that subjection, since they do not benefit from them in establishing oneness. The seeing is visual (basariyyah), and the seeing of the subjection is the seeing of its traces and signs.

It is also possible that the seeing is cognitive ('ilmiyyah) in the same way, and the address is to the polytheists, as in His saying, ﴿He created the heavens without pillars that you can see﴾ [Luqman: 10].

The bestowal of favours (isbagh al-ni'am) means multiplying them. The root of isbagh is making what is worn ample (sabigh), that is, complete in covering. From this comes the phrase "dir' sabighah" (a full coat of mail). Then it was borrowed for multiplying, because an ample thing contains much of what is made from it, such as links of mail or lengths of cloth. Then this usage spread until it equalled the literal sense, so it is said "sawabigh al-ni'am" (abundant favours).

And ni'mah (favour) is the benefit which its doer intends as a kindness to another.

Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Hafs on the authority of 'Asim, and Abu Ja'far read (ni'amahu) in the plural form of ni'mah, governed by the divine name pronoun; in the attribution to the pronoun of Allah there is an emphasis on these favours. The rest read (ni'mah) in the singular form; since the intended meaning is the genus, the singular and plural are equal in it.

The indefiniteness in them is for magnification, so both readings are equal in conveying the emphasis on what Allah has bestowed upon them.

(Outward and inward) is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) according to the reading of Nafi' and those with him, and as an adjective (sifah) according to the reading of the rest.

The outward (zahirah) is the manifest. The inward (batinah) is the hidden, and what is not known except by evidence, or not known at all.

The root meaning of batinah is what is lodged within the interior of a thing, that is, its inside. He, Exalted is He, said, ﴿Within it is mercy﴾ [al-Hadid: 13]. So in the human body and its conditions there are many favours: some people know them, some do not know them, some are known only to scholars, and some are not known by one generation but are later disclosed to those who come after. Both kinds include religious and worldly categories.

* * *

﴿And among people is one who disputes about Allah without knowledge or guidance or an illuminating book﴾ ﴿And when it is said to them, "Follow what Allah has sent down," they say, "Rather we follow what we found our fathers upon." Even if Satan was calling them to the punishment of the Blaze?﴾

The waw in His saying ﴿And among people is one who disputes﴾ is the waw of circumstance (hal). The meaning: you have seen that Allah subjected to you what is in the heavens and bestowed upon you abundant favours, while some of you dispute about the oneness of Allah and feign blindness to the proofs of His oneness. The circumstantial clause here is a statement used for expressing wonder at the condition of this group.

You may also make the waw parenthetical (i'tiradiyyah), with the clause interposed between the clause ﴿Have you not seen that Allah has subjected to you﴾ and the clause ﴿And if you asked them who created the heavens and the earth﴾ [Luqman: 25].

His saying (among people) uses the explicit noun in place of the pronoun, as if it were said "among you"; min is partitive. The intended group are those who set themselves to oppose the Prophet ﷺ in argument and to deceive their people, such as al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, Umayyah ibn Khalaf, and 'Abd Allah ibn al-Ziba'ra.

His saying ﴿without knowledge or guidance or an illuminating book﴾ covers the levels of acquiring knowledge, which are either: independent reasoning and acquisition (ijtihad and iktisab), or learning from a scholar, or reading sound books.

The interpretation of the parallel of this verse has already passed in Surah al-Hajj.

The clause (And when it is said to them, etc.) is conjoined to the relative clause of (among people, one who), meaning: this and that is their condition. The parallel of this clause has already occurred in Surah al-Baqarah.

The pronoun in His saying (calling them) refers to the fathers: that is, do they follow their fathers even if Satan was calling the fathers to punishment? They follow them to punishment and are not guided. (Even if) is a conditional particle of concession (law wasliyyah), and the waw with it is for circumstance.

The interrogative is for wonder at the enormity of their misguidance and blindness, to the degree that they follow whoever calls them to the Fire; and this is a censure of them. It is of the same pattern as His saying in the verse of al-Baqarah, ﴿Even though their fathers did not understand anything﴾ [al-Baqarah: 170]. The calling to the punishment of the Blaze means calling to its causes. The Blaze (al-sa'ir) was mentioned in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Whenever it dies down, We increase them in blaze﴾ [al-Isra: 97], in Surah al-Isra.

Then this usage spread until it equalled the literal sense, so it is said "sawabigh al-ni'am" (abundant favours).

And ni'mah (favour) is the benefit which its doer intends as a kindness to another.

Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Hafs on the authority of 'Asim, and Abu Ja'far read (ni'amahu) in the plural form of ni'mah, governed by the divine name pronoun; in the attribution to the pronoun of Allah there is an emphasis on these favours. The rest read (ni'mah) in the singular form; since the intended meaning is the genus, the singular and plural are equal in it.

The indefiniteness in them is for magnification, so both readings are equal in conveying the emphasis on what Allah has bestowed upon them.

(Outward and inward) is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) according to the reading of Nafi' and those with him, and as an adjective (sifah) according to the reading of the rest.

The outward (zahirah) is the manifest. The inward (batinah) is the hidden, and what is not known except by evidence, or not known at all.

The root meaning of batinah is what is lodged within the interior of a thing, that is, its inside. He, Exalted is He, said, ﴿Within it is mercy﴾ [al-Hadid: 13]. So in the human body and its conditions there are many favours: some people know them, some do not know them, some are known only to scholars, and some are not known by one generation but are later disclosed to those who come after. Both kinds include religious and worldly categories.

* * *

﴿And among people is one who disputes about Allah without knowledge or guidance or an illuminating book﴾ ﴿And when it is said to them, "Follow what Allah has sent down," they say, "Rather we follow what we found our fathers upon." Even if Satan was calling them to the punishment of the Blaze?﴾

The waw in His saying ﴿And among people is one who disputes﴾ is the waw of circumstance (hal). The meaning: you have seen that Allah subjected to you what is in the heavens and bestowed upon you abundant favours, while some of you dispute about the oneness of Allah and feign blindness to the proofs of His oneness. The circumstantial clause here is a statement used for expressing wonder at the condition of this group.

You may also make the waw parenthetical (i'tiradiyyah), with the clause interposed between the clause ﴿Have you not seen that Allah has subjected to you﴾ and the clause ﴿And if you asked them who created the heavens and the earth﴾ [Luqman: 25].

His saying (among people) uses the explicit noun in place of the pronoun, as if it were said "among you"; min is partitive. The intended group are those who set themselves to oppose the Prophet ﷺ in argument and to deceive their people, such as al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, Umayyah ibn Khalaf, and 'Abd Allah ibn al-Ziba'ra.

His saying ﴿without knowledge or guidance or an illuminating book﴾ covers the levels of acquiring knowledge, which are either: independent reasoning and acquisition (ijtihad and iktisab), or learning from a scholar, or reading sound books.

The interpretation of the parallel of this verse has already passed in Surah al-Hajj.

The clause (And when it is said to them, etc.) is conjoined to the relative clause of (among people, one who), meaning: this and that is their condition. The parallel of this clause has already occurred in Surah al-Baqarah.

The pronoun in His saying (calling them) refers to the fathers: that is, do they follow their fathers even if Satan was calling the fathers to punishment? They follow them to punishment and are not guided. (Even if) is a conditional particle of concession (law wasliyyah), and the waw with it is for circumstance.

The interrogative is for wonder at the enormity of their misguidance and blindness, to the degree that they follow whoever calls them to the Fire; and this is a censure of them. It is of the same pattern as His saying in the verse of al-Baqarah, ﴿Even though their fathers did not understand anything﴾ [al-Baqarah: 170]. The calling to the punishment of the Blaze means calling to its causes. The Blaze (al-sa'ir) was mentioned in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Whenever it dies down, We increase them in blaze﴾ [al-Isra: 97], in Surah al-Isra.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 31, verse 22:

﴿And whoever submits his face to Allah while being a doer of good has grasped the most reliable handhold. And to Allah is the outcome of all affairs.﴾

This is the counterpart of His saying ﴿And among the people is he who disputes about Allah without knowledge﴾ [Luqman: 20] up to His saying ﴿He invites them to the punishment of the Blaze﴾ [Luqman: 21]. Those are the ones who followed what they found their fathers upon of shirk, without insight, and so they fell into punishment. And these are the ones who did not cling to the religion of their fathers, and who submitted to Allah when He called them to Islam; neither the familiarity of custom nor the sanctity they gave their forefathers prevented them from following the truth. Those (the first group) clung to illusions and held fast to them to satisfy their desires, while these held fast to the truth seeking to satisfy the proof. Those pleased Satan, and these followed the pleasure of Allah.

The submission of the face to Allah is a metaphor for devoting worship exclusively to Him, as though one does not turn one's face toward other than Allah. This has already been discussed in His saying ﴿Yes, whoever submits his face to Allah while being a doer of good﴾ [al-Baqarah: 112] in Surat al-Baqarah, and His saying ﴿Then say: I have submitted my face to Allah﴾ [Al 'Imran: 20] in Surat Al 'Imran.

As for the verb yuslim being construed with a preposition here, without the lam as in the two verses of Surat al-Baqarah and Surat Al 'Imran, according to al-Zamakhshari it is a metaphor in the verb, by likening the person's very self to a commodity that its owner hands over to another and entrusts to him. Its literal form would be to construe it with lam, i.e., "his face," which is his very self, submitted (sāliman) ﴿to Allah﴾, i.e., sincerely devoted to Him, as in His saying ﴿And if they argue with you, then say: I have submitted my face to Allah﴾ [Al 'Imran: 20] in Surat Al 'Imran.

Ihsan (excellence) means righteous deed and sincerity in worship. In the hadith: "Ihsan is that you worship Allah as though you see Him; and if you do not see Him, indeed He sees you." The meaning: whoever submits with a submission free of hypocrisy and doubt, has taken hold of that by which he is safeguarded from desire or wavering.

As for His saying ﴿has grasped the most reliable handhold﴾, the discussion of its like has already passed at His saying ﴿Whoever disbelieves in false deities and believes in Allah has grasped the most reliable handhold﴾ [al-Baqarah: 256] in Surat al-Baqarah, and it is a commendation of the Muslims.

The concluding of this with His saying ﴿And to Allah is the outcome of all affairs﴾ is an allusion to the promise to them of meeting honour with Allah at the end of their affair, which is the Hereafter.

The definite article in "al-umur" (the affairs) is for comprehensiveness (istighraq), and it is a generalization by which is meant that the affairs of the Muslims, which fall within the scope of the general "affairs," return to Allah and are entrusted to Him; so their recompense with good is fitting to the majesty of Allah.

Al-'aqibah: the final state and the ultimate end.

Al-umur: plural of amr, which means matter or affair.

The fronting of (ilā Allāh) is for emphasis and to draw attention to the fact that whoever returns to Him meets his recompense in full.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 31, verse 23:

﴿And whoever disbelieves, let not his disbelief grieve you. To Us is their return, and We will inform them of what they did. Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what is within the breasts.﴾

When the condemnation of those who disbelieved, which was accompanied by threat, had passed, and the discourse moved from it to the praise of the Muslims and the promise to them, the discourse turned to consoling the Messenger (ﷺ), by making light of their disbelief toward him, as consolation for him and as an indirect indication that they were of little concern to him, because their return is to Allah, and He will show them the recompense appropriate to their disbelief. Thus it is an indirect threat to them.

The prohibition is ascribed to their disbelief in not being a cause of grief for the Messenger (ﷺ), a metaphorical ascription (majaz 'aqli) in the sense of prohibiting the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, from persistently dwelling in thought on grief over their disbelief, because when he removes that from his soul, the grieving over their disbelief ceases to affect him.

Nafi' read (يُحْزِنْكَ) with a dammah on the yaa' and a kasrah on the zay, the present tense of ahzana (to cause someone to grieve), meaning he made him grieving. The rest (of the readers) read (يَحْزُنْكَ) with a fathah on the yaa' and a dammah on the zay, the present tense of hazana (to grieve), with the same meaning. Both are dialects: the first is the dialect of Tamim, and the second is the dialect of Quraysh. The first is more analogical (aqyas), and both are eloquent (fasih). The dialect of Tamim is among the dialects in which the Qur'an was revealed, being the高 dialect of the upper Tamim, namely the Banu Darim, as was mentioned in the Sixth Introduction. Abu Zayd and al-Zamakhshari claimed that the widely-known usage is ahzana in the past and yuhzinu in the future, meaning the usage that is common on people's tongues; but the recitation is a transmitted report and a sunnah.

It was mentioned in Surah Yusuf: ﴿Indeed, it grieves me﴾ [Yusuf: 13], and in Surah al-An'am: ﴿We know indeed that what they say grieves you﴾ [al-An'am: 33].

The clause ﴿To Us is their return﴾ stands in the position of a reason for the prohibition. It is also a preparation for the promise to the Messenger (ﷺ) that Allah will take vengeance upon them, which is indicated by His saying ﴿so We will inform them﴾, which is a consequence of the clause ﴿To Us is their return﴾, as a kinaya for requital. The verb "inform" is used while its implication is intended, which is making it manifest, as was mentioned just before.

The clause ﴿Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what is within the breasts﴾ is a reason for the clause ﴿so We will inform them of what they did﴾. The position of the particle inna here serves in place of the fa' of causation, as in the saying of Bashshar:

"Indeed, that success lies in early rising..."

Dhat al-sudur (what is within the breasts) refers to intentions and the states of the soul such as resentment and the planning of deceit and disbelief. Its relevance here is that the disbelief of the polytheists is partly open declaration and partly concealment. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And keep your speech secret or declare it; indeed, He is Knowing of what is within the breasts﴾ [al-Mulk: 13]. It was mentioned in His saying ﴿Indeed, He is Knowing of what is within the breasts﴾ [al-Anfal: 43] in Surah al-Anfal.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 31, verse 24:

﴿We will let them enjoy themselves a little, then We will drive them to a harsh punishment.﴾

This is an explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani), because His saying ﴿To Us is their return, and We will inform them of what they did﴾ [Luqman: 23] raises in the minds of the listeners a question about why the requital is not hastened for them. So He clarifies that Allah gives them respite for a time, then casts them into a punishment from which they will find no escape. This resumption falls as an interjection between the conjoined sentences.

Al-tamti' (enjoyment) is the provision of a time-limited giving, so it is the bestowing of mata' (enjoyment), i.e., a little thing. Qalilan (a little) is an attribute of a verbal noun (masdar) of an absolute object, meaning tamti'an qalilan (a little enjoyment). Its littleness is either relative to what Allah has prepared for the believers, or due to the brevity of its duration in this world relative to the duration of the Hereafter. It was discussed earlier at His saying ﴿And there is enjoyment for a time﴾ [al-A'raf: 24] in Surat al-A'raf.

Al-idtirar (compulsion) is al-ilja' (forcing), which is making another party subject to necessity (darurah), i.e., obligation. It was discussed earlier at His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Then I will compel him to the punishment of the Fire﴾ [al-Baqarah: 126] in Surat al-Baqarah.

Al-ghalidh (harsh) is among the attributes of bodies, and it is that which is strong and coarse. It has been applied to the severe of states by way of metaphor (isti'arah), based on the common feature of severity upon the soul and the inability to bear it. His saying ﴿And We saved them from a harsh punishment﴾ [Hud: 58] was discussed earlier in Surat Hud, just as al-kathir (much) is applied to the strong.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 31, verse 25:

﴿And if you were to ask them, "Who created the heavens and the earth?" they would surely say, "Allah." Say, "Praise be to Allah." But most of them do not know.﴾

This is a continuation (ʿatf) of the statement ﴿And when it is said to them, "Follow what Allah has sent down," they say, "Rather, we will follow what we found our fathers upon."﴾ [Luqman: 21], in that what they found their fathers upon is associating others with Allah in divinity. And if a questioner were to ask them, "Who created the heavens and the earth?", they would say, "Allah created them." This is a belittling of their intellects, which combine acknowledging that Allah is the Creator with believing in the divinity of other than Him.

By "the heavens and the earth" is meant what includes what is in them of created beings, and among that the stones of the idols. A similar usage has preceded in Surat al-Ankabut. Here he expressed it as ﴿do not know﴾ (lā yaʿlamūn), while in Surat al-ʿAnkabut he expressed it as ﴿do not reason﴾ (lā yaʿqilūn), as a variation in wording between the two narratives while the meaning remains the same.

[p. 180]

﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth. Indeed, Allah is the Free of need, the Praiseworthy.﴾

The position of this sentence relative to the one before it is that of the conclusion relative to the proof, in His words ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens﴾. Therefore it is separated from what precedes it and not joined by a conjunction, because it stands in the position of badal al-ishtimal (inclusive apposition) to the preceding sentence, as was mentioned just before in His words ﴿He will bring it forth. Indeed, Allah is Subtle and Acquainted﴾ [Luqman: 16]. When their acknowledgment that Allah created the heavens and the earth was established, it necessarily followed that whatever is in the heavens and the earth belongs to Allah, and among that are their idols. The explicit statement of this conclusion is intended to belittle them in their disbelief, by [showing] that Allah owns them and owns whatever is in the heavens and the earth, so He is Free of need from their worship and Praiseworthy apart from them.

The pronoun "huwa" (هو) is a damir al-fasl (separating pronoun), whose implication is the restriction of self-sufficiency and praise to Allah, the Exalted. It is a qasr al-qalb (restriction by reversal), meaning: their supposed gods have no self-sufficiency, and they do not deserve praise.

The discussion of "al-Ghaniyy al-Hamid" (the Free of need, the Praiseworthy) has already occurred at His words ﴿Indeed, Allah is Free of need and Praiseworthy﴾ [Luqman: 12] at the beginning of the surah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 31, verse 27:

﴿And if whatever trees are on the earth were pens, and the sea, with seven more seas to supplement it, were ink, the words of Allah would not be exhausted. Indeed, Allah is Mighty and Wise.﴾

The attribute of Allah as encompassing all things, apparent and hidden, has been repeated in what preceded in this surah. He said, in what He related of the counsel of Luqman, ﴿Indeed, if it be an atom's weight, from a mustard seed﴾ [Luqman: 16], up to His saying ﴿Subtle, Acquainted﴾ [Luqman: 16]. And He said after that, ﴿Then We will inform them of what they did. Indeed, Allah is Knowing of that within the breasts﴾ [Luqman: 23]. So He followed that with establishing that the knowledge of Allah the Exalted has manifestations, some of which He conveys to whomever He chooses from among His messengers by revelation, as wisdom requires conveying it, and that He keeps to Himself the knowledge of what His wisdom requires not be conveyed. And that if He willed to convey what is in His knowledge, His created things, which are fit to record His speech by writing, would not be sufficient for it, let alone be sufficient for conveying that by means of speech. He followed in this the path of bringing it closer through striking this parable. What had been related of the accounts of past peoples had already paved the way for this. The story of Luqman in this surah occurs just as the story of the People of the Cave and Dhu al-Qarnayn occurs in Surah al-Kahf, and both were followed, at the end of that surah, by His saying ﴿Say: If the sea were ink for the words of my Lord, the sea would be exhausted before the words of my Lord are exhausted, even if We brought the like of it as a supplement﴾ [al-Kahf: 109], which is similar to the verse in Surah Luqman. This is the aspect of the connection of this verse with the scattered verses before it.

Because the connection of the verse with what precedes it is obscure, the early interpreters among the companions of Ibn 'Abbas took up the explanation of the placement of this verse in this position. It has been said: the occasion of its revelation is what al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyyah and al-Wahidi mentioned from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, 'Ikrimah and 'Ata' ibn Yasar, in closely similar narrations: "The Jews asked the Messenger of Allah, or the Quraysh were incited by them to ask him, when they heard the saying of Allah the Exalted concerning them: ﴿They ask you about the soul. Say: The soul is of the command of my Lord, and you have not been given of knowledge except a little﴾ [al-Isra: 85]. They said: How, when you recite in what has come to you that we have been given the Torah, and in it is the clarification of everything? The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to those who asked him: It is, in the knowledge of Allah, a little. Then Allah revealed ﴿And if whatever trees are on the earth were pens﴾, the two verses, or the three verses."

And from al-Suddi: The Quraysh said: How much Muhammad talks! So this verse was revealed: ﴿And if whatever trees are on the earth were pens﴾, the verse.

And from Qatadah: The Quraysh said: This speech will end for Muhammad and he will be exhausted (i.e., Muhammad ﷺ), so he will not say any speech after it. In another narration: This speech will be exhausted. Some of these reports go back to the view that this verse was revealed in Medina, which entails that its placement in this position in the surah is by prophetic direction, for the reason we mentioned just now. Others go back to the view that it is Meccan, which requires that it was revealed during the revelation of Surah Luqman, to be placed after the verses revealed before it.

The word kalimat is the plural of kalimah in the sense of speech, as in His saying the Exalted ﴿No! It is but a word he is saying﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 100], meaning the speech that informs of the will of Allah concerning some of His creatures, by which He addresses His angels and others among the creatures and the elements counted for existence, to which it is said "Be," and it is. Among that is what He sent down of revelation to His messengers and prophets from the earliest times of the prophets, and what He will send down to His Messenger ﷺ. That is, if it were assumed that Allah's will was to write down all His speech in pages, then all the trees would be assumed divided into pens, and the sea assumed to be ink, and with those pens and that ink He wrote, the sea would be exhausted and the pens would be used up, and the words of Allah would not be exhausted in reality.

As for His saying the Exalted (﴿And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth and justice﴾ [al-An'am: 115]), the fulfilment there means realisation and taking effect. His saying the Exalted ﴿And Allah wills to establish the truth by His words﴾ [al-Anfal: 7] has already occurred in Surah al-Anfal.

This verse has been arranged with wondrous brevity, for it begins with the particle law, so it is understood that its content is a supposed matter. The particle law has uses, as verified in Mughni al-Labib, drawing on the wording of Sibawayh. It has already been discussed at His saying the Exalted ﴿And if He had made them hear, they would have turned away while they were averting﴾ [al-Anfal: 23] in Surah al-Anfal.

The phrase ﴿min shajarah﴾ is an explanation of the relative ma, and it has the sense of a specification (tamyiz), so its rule is the singular, and for this reason He did not say "min ashjar." Al-aqlam is the plural of qalam, which is a split piece of wood used to hold ink and write with. That is, if every tree became pens in the amount of its branches suitable for that. Al-aqlam is the common plural of qalam, and it occurs for both the many and the few.

As for yamudduhu, with a fatha on the ya' and a damma on the mim, it means "increases it in ink." Al-midad, with a kasra on the mim, is the ink with which one writes. It is said: madda al-dawah yamuddu-ha (he supplied the inkwell). So His saying yamuddu-hu includes the supposition that the sea is ink, then seven seas are added to it when its ink dries up. Had it been said yumiddu-hu, with a damma on the mim from amadda, this conciseness would have been lost.

The number seven is often used as a metaphor for abundance, like the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "The disbeliever eats in seven intestines." So there is no restricted meaning to this number; that is, the sea is supplied by many seas.

The meaning of ﴿mā nafidat kalimātu-llāh﴾ is "were not finished." That is, how can the Jews reckon that what is in the Torah is the limit of the words of Allah, or how can the polytheists reckon that what has been sent down of the Qur'an is about to be the end of the Qur'an? On this second aspect, the parable comes as an exaggeration of the abundance of what will yet be sent down of the Qur'an, as vexation to the polytheists. Thus "the words of Allah" would be the Qur'an, because the polytheists do not know the words of Allah, which cannot be encompassed.

The clause ﴿Indeed, Allah is Mighty and Wise﴾ is a concluding clause. He, by His might, is not overcome by those who claim there is no need for the Qur'an and await the silencing of the Messenger ﷺ; and He, by His wisdom, has words that are not limited, for true wisdom has no end.

The majority read ﴿wa-l-baḥru﴾ with a nominative (raf') on "al-bahr," on the basis that the nominal clause is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), and the waw is the waw of circumstance, and it is a circumstance of ﴿anna-mā fi al-arḍi min shajarah﴾, meaning: those trees exist while the sea is ink for them. The waw achieves through it a linking and a sufficiency without needing a pronoun, since it indicates concomitance.

Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read ﴿wa-l-baḥra﴾ with the accusative (nasb), as a conjunction upon the noun of inna.

The sentence is an explanatory resumptive clause (*isti'naf bayani*, a clause that answers an unstated question) connected to His words, ﴿To Us is their return, and We will inform them of what they did﴾ [Luqman: 23], because whenever the mention of resurrection occurs, the thought that re-creating bodies after they have decayed is impossible arises in the minds of the polytheists. Therefore the Qur'an often follows the mention of resurrection with an indication of its possibility and nearness.

They also used to say: God created us in stages: a drop, then a clinging clot, then a lump of flesh, then bone and flesh. So how will He resurrect us as a new creation in a single hour, and how will He bring back all the nations and generations that the earth has contained over many centuries? Ubayy ibn Khalaf, Abu al-Asad (or Abu al-Asadayn), and Nubayh and Munabbih, the sons of al-Hajjaj of the clan of Sahm, used to say this, and perhaps some of them confided it secretly.

The two pronouns of address are intended to refer to all creation, so they stand for the genus. That is, the creation of all people the first time, and their resurrection, meaning their creation a second time, is nothing but like the creation of a single soul. This is because the creation of a single soul in this wondrous manner indicates the complete power of the Creator, Exalted is He. When the One who is perfect in power is in question, few and many, beginning and returning, are equal with respect to His power.

In His words ﴿your creation and your resurrection﴾ there is an *iltifat* (a shift from the third person to the second person) in order to confront them with the decisive argument.

In His words ﴿like a single soul﴾ a genitive noun has been omitted, which is indicated by ﴿your creation and your resurrection﴾. The sense is: "except like the creation and resurrection of a single soul." This is conciseness (*ijaz*), like the words of al-Nabigha:

*And I have feared so much that my fear does not exceed
the fear of a wild bull in the thicket of Mutarah, alert.*

The meaning is: "like the fear of a wild bull."

The intended meaning is that the second creation is like the first creation in terms of power.

The clause ﴿Indeed God is All-Hearing, All-Seeing﴾ is either placed as a causal justification for the complete power over that wondrous creation, by way of argument from the comprehensiveness of His knowledge of things, their causes, their details and their particulars. It is the nature of the knower to act upon what is known as he wills, because incapacity to bring about some of what the will is directed toward arises from the obscurity of the cause that leads to its bringing into existence. Since the polytheists, or their intellectuals, accepted that God knows everything, their acceptance of this was made a means of persuading them of His power over everything.

Or it is placed as a resumptive explanatory clause (*istinaf bayani*) for what arises from the report that their resurrection is like a single soul, from the astonishment of a group among those who concealed in their souls the denial of resurrection, those to whom His earlier words alluded: ﴿Indeed God knows what is in the breasts﴾ [Luqman: 23]. For this reason He did not say "Indeed God is All-Knowing, All-Powerful."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 31, verse 29:

﴿Have you not seen that Allah causes the night to enter into the day and causes the day to enter into the night, and has subjected the sun and the moon, each running to a specified term, and that Allah is Acquainted with what you do?﴾

This is an argument for what the preceding verse contained, namely that the second creation, which is the resurrection, lies within the scope of Allah's power. It is argued that He is capable of changing the states of what is greater in state than man, namely by changing the states of the earth and its horizon between night and day in every day and night. This change resembles the onset of death upon life in the entry of night into day, and the onset of life upon death in the entry of day into night. It is also argued that He is capable of something greater than that, through what He has subjected of the courses of the sun and the moon.

This argument for the possibility of resurrection is by analogy of similitude (qiyas al-tamthil, reasoning by analogy from a similar case) to the possibility of things greater than it among the affairs of created beings. It follows an earlier argument by a universal analogy (qiyas kulli) which was required by His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah is Hearing and Seeing﴾ [Luqman: 28], from the comprehensiveness of divine knowledge over the known things, which requires the comprehensiveness of His power over the possible things, since these are particulars of the known things and branch from them.

The address is to an unspecified audience, and the intended people are the polytheists, by the indication of ﴿and that Allah is Acquainted with what you do﴾.

The seeing (ru'ya) is intellectual (ilmiyyah). The interrogative is for denying the non-seeing, by treating those who have knowledge as though they lacked it, because they do not benefit from their knowledge.

Al-iylaj (ال إيلاج) means causing to enter. Here it is a figure for the alternation of darkness and light, by the entry of one of them into the other, as in His saying ﴿And a sign for them is the night; We strip from it the day﴾ [Ya-Sin: 37].

The discussion of its counterpart in His saying ﴿He causes the night to enter into the day﴾ [Al 'Imran: 27] was already presented at the beginning of Al 'Imran, and in His saying ﴿That is because Allah causes the night to enter into the day﴾ [al-Hajj: 61], the verse in Surat al-Hajj, though the purposes differ.

The beginning is with the night because its matter is more wondrous: how its darkness overcomes those daytime lights. The combination of the entry of the night and the entry of the day is to show the perfection of power, such that one does not necessitate a similar action.

The discussion of the subjection of the sun and the moon has passed in Surat al-A'raf.

The tanwin of (كل) (kull) is what is called tanwin al-'iwad (the nunation that replaces an omitted element), in place of the noun it is annexed to. The estimate is: each one of the sun and the moon runs to a term.

Al-jary (الجري) is quick walking. It is borrowed for the movement of the sun in its orbit, the movement of the earth around the sun, and the movement of the moon around the earth, as a likeness to quick walking because of the vastness of the distances covered in the course of that.

The addition of His saying ﴿to a specified term﴾ indicates that this solar system has a span which Allah knows. When that span ends, that motion and movement cease. That is the time which announces the extinction of the world. So this is a reminder of the time of resurrection.

Thus (إلى أجل) may be a loose adverbial phrase (zarf laghw) connected to the verb (يجري), meaning that its running ends, that is, its course stops, at a specific term fixed with Allah for the ending of their course.

It may also be that (إلى أجل) is connected to the verb (سخر), meaning that He made the system of subjecting the sun and the moon end at a determined term.

The particle (إلى) in both estimates is for termination (lil-intiha').
