﴿And that Allah is Acquainted with what you do﴾ is conjoined to ﴿that Allah causes the night to enter into the day﴾. So it falls within the denying interrogative, by treating the one who has knowledge as other than one who has it, because they do not act according to what this knowledge requires. They know that Allah is Acquainted with what they do, yet they do not conform to what this knowledge requires in any of their states.

**Commentary of Ibn ʿĀshūr (al-Taḥrīr wa-l-Tanwīr) on Surah 31 (Luqmān), verse 30:**

﴿That is because Allah is the Truth, and what they call upon besides Him is the false, and because Allah is the Most High, the Most Great.﴾

The *kāf* of address (*kāf al-khiṭāb*) attached to the demonstrative (*ism al-ishāra*) is addressed to an unspecified listener, and the intended audience is the polytheists. This is indicated by the phrase ﴿and what you call upon besides Him is the false﴾, which uses the second-person *tāʾ* in the recitation of Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr, Ibn ʿĀmir, and Abū Bakr on the authority of ʿĀṣim. The thing pointed to by the demonstrative is what was mentioned just before it, namely the interpolation (*al-īlāj*) of night and day and the subjugation (*al-taskhīr*) of the sun and moon.

The position of this sentence is that of a conclusion (*natīja*) drawn from the proof, so it has the status of an inclusive apposition (*badal al-ishtimāl*) of the demonstrative. For this reason it is detached (*fuṣilat*) and not joined by a conjunction (*lam tuʿṭaf*), since they acknowledge that Allah is the One who does that, and so the proof and its conclusion are binding upon them.

The meaning is: the interpolation of night into day and the reverse, and the subjugation of the sun and moon, are caused by Allah's exclusive divinity (*infirād Allāh bi-l-ilāhiyya*). Accordingly, the *bāʾ* is causal (*li-l-sababiyya*), and the phrase it introduces is a stable adverbial complement (*ẓarf mustaqarr*) functioning as the predicate of the demonstrative.

The separating pronoun (*ḍamīr al-faṣl*), which is the pronoun *huwa* in ﴿Allah is the Truth﴾, indicates exclusivity (*li-l-ikhtiṣāṣ*): that is, He is the Truth, not your idols nor anything else that is claimed to be divine besides Him, may He be exalted.

[p. 187]

Here *al-ḥaqq* means "the established/ the firm," and it is understood that what is intended is the truth of the establishment of His divinity, by the context and by its contrast with the phrase ﴿and what you call upon besides Him is the false﴾. The meaning is: since that wondrous creation is caused by Allah's exclusive divinity, that creation is also a proof of Allah's exclusive divinity, because of the mutual implication (*talāzum*) between cause and effect. The definite article in *al-ḥaqq* and *al-bāṭil* is the definite article of the genus (*taʿrīf al-jins*).

The separating pronoun was not used in the second clause because what they call upon besides Allah, namely their idols, shares with them the quality of being false. The separating pronoun was used in its parallel in Surah al-Ḥajj because the context required it, as has already been explained.

It is apparent that if we take the *bāʾ* in ﴿Because Allah is the Truth﴾ as causal, then the phrase ﴿and that what you call upon besides Him is the false﴾ is a coordination (*ʿaṭf*) on the predicate, which is the whole construction introduced by ﴿because Allah﴾.

The implied sense is: that is because what you call upon besides Him is false. A suitable preposition that fits the meaning is omitted before *anna*, and that preposition indicates "on account of that." This is like the omission of the preposition *ʿan* in His words, exalted is He, ﴿and you desire to marry them﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 127]. It cannot be a coordination on the complement of the causal *bāʾ*, since the falsehood of their gods has no effect on the interpolation of night into day or on the subjugation of the sun and moon. Alternatively, the *lām* of cause may be understood, meaning: that is, because what you call upon is false. Therefore, what they call upon has no share in the interpolation of night and day or the subjugation of the sun and moon, by the acknowledgment of the polytheists.

His words ﴿and that Allah is the Most High, the Most Great﴾ stand in the position of a summation (*fadhlaka*) of what preceded, namely the indication of the interpolation of night and day and the subjugation of the sun and moon. For once it is established that what was mentioned indicates that Allah is the Truth in divinity, and indicates that what they call upon is false, it follows that He is the Most High, the Most Great, and not their idols. The separating pronoun is brought in here to indicate exclusivity and to deny loftiness and greatness to their idols.

It is better to take the *bāʾ* as expressing accompaniment or association (*li-l-mulābasa aw al-muṣāḥaba*), and then it is a stable adverbial complement functioning as the predicate of the demonstrative. The nature of the *bāʾ* of association is that it is a stable adverbial complement. Indeed, al-Raḍī said that it is only ever like this, meaning that it is only attached to something like a predicate or a circumstantial complement (*ḥāl*), as in the verse:

*"And for me, by the praise of Allah, there is no flesh nor blood."*

That is, in the state of my being associated with the praise of Allah, meaning not discontented with His decree. It is also said: "You are with the better of the two views," meaning "you are in a settled state."

So the sense is: that mentioned act of interpolation and subjugation is associated with the truth of Allah's divinity, exalted is He. The two conjoined elements are coordinated on the object of the *bāʾ*, meaning: it is associated with Allah being the true God, and with what you call upon besides Him being false in divinity, and with Allah being the Most High, the Most Great. The association expressed by the *bāʾ* is the association of the proof with what it proves. By this, the construction is sound without strain, and the placement of the sentence ﴿because Allah is the Truth﴾ to its end in the position of a conclusion becomes even clearer.

The separating pronoun in His words ﴿and that Allah is the Most High, the Most Great﴾ is for exclusivity, as was explained earlier in His words ﴿Indeed Allah is the Self-Sufficient, the Praiseworthy﴾ [Luqmān: 26].

*Al-ʿAlī* (the Most High) is an attributive adjective derived from figurative, non-physical loftiness, which is sanctity and nobility. *Al-Kabīr* (the Most Great) is an attributive adjective derived from figurative greatness, which is grandeur of standing. A parallel to this verse has already been mentioned in Surah al-Ḥajj, with the addition of the separating pronoun in His words ﴿and that what you call upon besides Him is the false, and that﴾.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 31, verses 31–32:

﴿Have you not seen that the ships sail on the sea by the favor of God, that He may show you some of His signs? Indeed, in that are signs for every steadfast, grateful person.﴾ ﴿And when a wave covers them like canopies, they call upon God, sincerely devoted to Him in religion. But when He delivers them to the land, some of them are moderate. None denies Our signs except every treacherous ingrate.﴾

This is a new resumptive sentence (*istinaf*), following the pattern of the two resumptive sentences before it, in His words ﴿Have you not seen that God has subjected to you what is in the heavens and what is in the earth?﴾ [Luqman: 20] and His words ﴿Have you not seen that God causes the night to enter the day?﴾ [Luqman: 29]. It is introduced without a conjunction, so that the hearer does not suppose that it is coordinated with what came between them. This third resumptive sentence is a third proof of the great wisdom of God in the order of this world, and of His granting humankind success in benefiting from what God has prepared for their benefit.

When the first two resumptive sentences had dealt with the evidences of God's craftsmanship in the heavens and the earth, this third one brings a proof of the wondrous craftsmanship of God in creating the sea and making it easy to benefit from in establishing the order of human society. It moves from this to the way a group of people take the causes of gratitude as occasions for disbelief.

The creation of the sea in this great form made travel on it possible, at times when land routes do not suffice for transport. He made it capable of bearing great ships, and inspired human beings to build those ships in a manner that protects them from drowning in the surging depths of the sea. He preserved them from the successive winds and waves during their voyages, and guided them to the means of coping with these when they arise, until they pass. For this reason, He described this sailing as accompanied by God's favor, for whenever ships carry people on the sea, they are usually in a state of being favored by God with safety, except in rare circumstances. This favor is called a command (*amr*) in His words ﴿and the ships sail on the sea by His command﴾ [al-Hajj: 65] in Surah al-Hajj, that is, by His decree and the order of His creation.

Its detail has been discussed earlier in His words ﴿Then when they board the ships﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 65] in Surah al-'Ankabut, and in His words ﴿It is He who enables you to travel on land and sea﴾ [Yunus: 22] and the verses after it in Surah Yunus, and in His words ﴿Have you not seen that God has subjected to you what is in the earth, and the ships that sail on the sea by His command?﴾ [al-Hajj: 65] in Surah al-Hajj.

The phrase *li-yurikum* (that He may show you) is connected to *tajri* (sail), meaning: the sailing of the ships on the sea is a sailing, and the cause of its creation is that God may show you some of His signs. He did not mention the object of the signs (i.e., what they are signs of), because it is evident from *li-yurikum*. The sailing of the ships on the sea is one of the signs of power in wondrous craftsmanship: He created the water of the sea with an order, created wood with an order, and gave human minds an order. From all of this there results the possibility of the ship's movement over the surging depths of the sea.

The meaning is that the sailing of ships on the sea has many wise purposes intended by His subjecting it, among them that it be a sign for people of the existence of the Creator, His oneness, His knowledge and His power.

The *lam* of causation (*lam al-ta'lil*) does not require that the purpose of the thing caused be restricted to what follows it, because causes are partial, not total.

The clause ﴿Indeed, in that are signs for every steadfast, grateful person﴾ serves as a causal explanation of the clause *yurikum min ayatihi* (that He may show you some of His signs). It also serves as an explanatory resumption (*istinaf bayani*), since the hearer may come to mind asking: how is it that the polytheists were not guided by these signs? So it is stated that the one who benefits from their indication of what they signify is the ﴿every steadfast, grateful person﴾, explicitly praising this group and implicitly reproaching those who did not benefit from their indication.

The clause is joined with the particle *inna* because in such a context it conveys the meaning of causation and attribution.

He made these "signs" plural because there are many indications in it, that is, those who are never without these two qualities.

*Al-sabbar* is an intensive form of the one characterized by patience, and *al-shakur* is likewise, that is, those who are never without these two qualities. These are two attributes of the monotheist believers: patience in adversity and gratitude in prosperity, since they hope through these for the pleasure of God Exalted, upon whom alone they rely in removing harm and increasing good. They have cultivated these qualities through what they heard of the encouragement to these two attributes and the warning against their opposites. He said ﴿and the patient in hardship, adversity and the time of battle﴾ [al-Baqarah: 177], and He said ﴿If you are grateful, I will surely increase you﴾ [Ibrahim: 7]. Thus they are between hope for reward and fear of punishment, because they believe in the eternal life with recompense, and know that their final return is to God, who commands and forbids. These qualities became for them a disposition they were shaped by, so that they never or only rarely leave them. As for the polytheists, their outlook is confined to the present life, so they are captives of the sensory world. When harm reaches them they become distressed, and when benefit reaches them they become insolent. Thus they are devoid of patience and gratitude. For this reason His words ﴿for every steadfast, grateful person﴾ are a symbolic metonymy (*kinaya ramziyya*) for the believers, and a symbolic implicit reproach (*ta'rid ramzi*) directed at the polytheists.

The reason for choosing the two qualities of patience and gratitude here as metonymies for them is that they are among the branches of faith, and that they are most appropriate to the context of sailing on the sea, since the sea traveler is between danger and safety, and these two are the manifestation of patience and gratitude, as was mentioned earlier in His words ﴿It is He who enables you to travel on land and sea, until when you are in the ships﴾ [Yunus: 22], the verse in Surah Yunus.

In His words ﴿for every steadfast, grateful person﴾ there is a graceful transition (*husn al-takhallus*) to the detail that He follows in His words ﴿And when a wave covers them like canopies﴾ and the verse that follows. It is joined to the verses about the sailing of ships, indicating that people remember God at those signs when they are compelled, and forget them in the state of safety. The same was mentioned earlier in His words in Surah al-'Ankabut ﴿Then when they board the ships, they call upon God, sincerely devoted to Him in religion. But when He delivers them to the land, behold, they associate partners [with Him]﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 65], and in His words in Surah Yunus ﴿until when you are in the ships and they sail with them on a favorable wind﴾ [Yunus: 22] and the verses that follow.

*Al-ghashayan* (covering) is used metaphorically for "coming," because it resembles covering. It has been discussed earlier in His words ﴿He covers the night over the day﴾ [al-A'raf: 54] in Surah al-A'raf.

*Al-zulal*, with a *dammah* on the *zay* and a *fathah* on the *lam*, is the plural of *zullah* (with a *dammah*), which means what overshadows of clouds.

The *fa'* in His words ﴿So among them is a moderate one﴾ indicates an implied element, as if it were said: "When He delivered them, they divided; so among them is a moderate one, and among them is other than that," as will come. Ibn Malik held that the *fa'* enters upon the response of *lamma* (when), that is, as a connecting particle for the response. Those who disagree with him prohibit the response of *lamma* from being joined with *fa'*, as in *Mughni al-Labib*.

*Al-muqtasid* is the one who practices *qasd*, which is moderation between two extremes. The context indicates that what is meant is moderation in disbelief, because the verse is concluded with His words ﴿None denies Our signs except every treacherous ingrate﴾, and because of His words in a parallel verse in Surah al-'Ankabut ﴿But when He delivers them to the land, behold, they associate partners [with Him]﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 65]. The term *muqtasid* may also be applied to one whose state falls midway between righteousness and its opposite, as He said ﴿Among them is a moderate community, but many of them, evil is what they do﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 66].

*Al-jahid al-kafur* is the one who is excessive in disbelief and denial. *Al-juhud* means denial and negation, and it was discussed earlier at His words ﴿But the wrongdoers deny the signs of God﴾ [al-An'am: 33] in Surah al-An'am. It is known that there is a third category, namely the one who is certain of the signs and grateful for the favor. These are the believers. He said in Surah Fatir ﴿So among them is one who wrongs himself, and among them is one who is moderate, and among them is one who is foremost in good deeds﴾ [Fatir: 32]. This restriction (*iqtisar*) is like the verse of Jarir:

"Hanifah were in thirds: a third of them were slaves, and a third were their clients."

That is, the remaining third were of their own kin.

*Al-khattar* is one who is intensely treacherous, and *al-khatr* is the most severe treachery.

The clause ﴿None denies Our signs except every treacherous ingrate﴾ to its end is a generalizing conclusion (*tadhyil*), because it encompasses every denier, whether one who denies the sailing of ships and the terror of the sea and denies God's favor upon him in deliverance, or one who denies other than that of God's signs and favors. The meaning is: "Among them is one who denies Our signs."

The shift from the third person (*al-ghayba*) to the first person (*al-takallum*) in His words *bi-ayatina* (Our signs) is an *iltifat* (shift of grammatical person).

The *ba'* in *bi-ayatina* is for emphasizing the transitivity of the verb to its object, as in His words ﴿and wipe your heads﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 6], and the verse of al-Nabighah:

"Yours is the goodness, if the earth should conceal you, one alone..."

and His words ﴿We send the signs only as a warning﴾ [al-Isra': 59].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 31, verse 33:

﴿O mankind, fear your Lord and dread a Day when no parent will avail anything for his child, nor will a child avail anything for his parent. Indeed, the promise of Allah is true. So let not the worldly life deceive you, and let not the Deceiver deceive you concerning Allah.﴾

If "O mankind" is not a address specific to the polytheists, then it is general to all people, as has been established in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh). It thus includes the believer, the polytheist, and the one who denies (divine attributes) at that time and in all other times, since all of them are commanded to have taqwa of Allah, and the steps that lead to taqwa vary according to the varying distance of those who travel toward it. Since in what preceded in the surah there were portions for the believers and portions for the polytheists, it is not far-fetched that it be followed by something suitable for both groups. And if the address is specific to the polytheists, in accordance with what has been narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that "O mankind" is an address to the people of Makkah, then the meaning of taqwa is abandoning polytheism.

The placement of this verse after the verses preceding it is like the placement of the aim of a sermon after its introductions, since the preceding introductions had prepared souls to accept guidance and to be affected by good admonition. Wise people have opportunities for catching (the attention of hearers) and they are eager not to waste them. The best example of this is the words of al-Hariri in the Eleventh Maqama: (When they had buried the dead, and the saying "would that" had passed, a shaykh appeared from a mound, leaning on a staff, and said: "For the like of this let the workers work. Remember, O heedless ones; hasten, O negligent ones.") etc. As for hard hearts and disobedient souls, no healer will cure them.

And for the sake of considering this placement, the sentence was made a resumption (isti'naf), because it stands in the position of a summary (fadhlaka) and a conclusion.

Taqwa begins with acknowledging the existence of the Creator and His oneness, and affirming the Messenger ﷺ, and it ends in avoiding what is forbidden and carrying out what is commanded, outwardly and inwardly, in all circumstances. Its detailed explanation was given earlier at His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿guidance for the God-fearing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2] in Surat al-Baqarah, and a parallel of this was given earlier in Surat al-Hajj.

The fear of the Day is dread of the terrors that will occur in it, since time itself is not feared in its own right; hence "yawman" is in the accusative as an object. The command to fear it implies its occurrence, so it is a kinaya for affirming the Resurrection. The portion of the polytheists from this is that they do not believe in it, until it became a mark upon them. Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And those who do not expect to meet Us say﴾ [al-Furqan: 21].

The clause ﴿no parent will avail anything for his child﴾ and so on is an attribute of "yawm," and the returning pronoun in the prepositional phrase with (fi) has been omitted, as a broadening, by treating it like an accusative returning pronoun, as in His saying ﴿and fear a Day when no soul will avail anything for another soul﴾ [al-Baqarah: 48] in Surat al-Baqarah.

Jaza, when transitive with (an), means "to settle on behalf of" and "to repel from," and for this reason the litigant is called al-mutajazi.

The clause (wa la mawlud) and so on is conjoined to the attribute; "mawlud" is the subject, and (huwa) is a separating pronoun (damir fasl). "Jaza" is the predicate of the subject.

The mention of parent and child here is because they are the most intense in love and protectiveness compared to others, so it is known that others are more deserving of this negation. Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿on the Day a man will flee from his brother﴾ [Abasa: 34] ﴿and his mother and his father﴾ [Abasa: 35], and so on.

It begins with "the parent" because he is more compassionate toward his child, so he finds no escape for him from harm except by doing it himself.

The reason for choosing this method for conveying the generality of the negation here, rather than the method of His saying ﴿and fear a Day when no soul will avail anything for another soul﴾ [al-Baqarah: 48] in Surat al-Baqarah, is that this verse was revealed in Makkah, and its people at that time were a mixture of Muslims and disbelievers; perhaps the father was a Muslim and the child a disbeliever, or perhaps the reverse. Some disbelievers, when doubts enter them about their fate after death, may imagine that if the threat of the Qur'an against them is shown to be true, whoever has a Muslim father or a Muslim son will be defended by him then, through what indicates the Lord of this religion. It was firmly established among the Arabs to rely on the patron and the helper, relying on the fact that zeal and pride would push them to defend one another in that gathering, even if they had previously been at odds, due to the narrowness of their understanding, measuring matters by their customs.

This is also the reason for combining the negation of a parent's recompense for his child with the negation of a child's recompense for his parent, so that it includes both groups in both situations, so that it is not imagined that one of the two groups is more hopeful regarding the intended meaning.

Then the clause ﴿nor will a child avail anything for his parent﴾ was chosen with forms of emphasis that the clause ﴿no parent will avail anything for his child﴾ does not contain, for it was arranged as a nominal sentence, the separating pronoun was placed in its midst, and the negation was directed at the category. The point of this choice is to intensify the affirmation that no part of this group can avail the other, since most of the believers were sons and youths, while their fathers and mothers were mostly upon polytheism, such as Abu Quhafa, the father of Abu Bakr; Abu Talib, the father of 'Ali; the mother of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas; and the mother of Asma' bint Abi Bakr. So it was intended to cut off the hopes of their fathers, and whatever hopes they might have of benefiting their parents in the Hereafter.

Here it is expressed as (mawlud) rather than (walad), to indicate the derivational meaning of "mawlud," unlike "walad," which is a noun functioning like a fixed noun, for the purpose of alerting that such a tender bond does not entitle its possessor to seek to benefit his polytheist father in the Hereafter, in fulfillment of what the state of being born (mawludiyya) implies of the hardship of raising him. Perhaps he would then strive insistently to avail on his behalf in the Hereafter, so as to cut off his hope of being availed. This is a reversal of the worldly tenderness in His saying ﴿And say, "My Lord, have mercy upon them as they brought me up when I was small"﴾ [al-Isra': 24] and His saying ﴿and accompany them in this world with kindness﴾ [Luqman: 15].

The clause ﴿Indeed, the promise of Allah is true﴾ is a cause (ʿilla) for the two clauses ﴿fear your Lord and dread a Day﴾. The promise of Allah is the Resurrection, as He said: ﴿And they say, "When is this promise, if you should be truthful?"﴾ [Yunus: 48] ﴿Say, "For you is an appointment of a Day you will not delay from by an hour, nor advance"﴾ [Saba': 30].

The statement was emphasized with (inna) in consideration of those who deny the Resurrection, since their doubt about denying it was the sight of people dying, and other generations succeeding them, and none of those who died returning. ﴿And they said, "There is not but our worldly life; we die and live, and nothing destroys us except time"﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 24] and they said ﴿There is not but our worldly life, and we will not be resurrected﴾ [al-An'am: 29].

Following this emphasis, the refutation of their doubt is made consequent by His saying ﴿So let not the worldly life deceive you﴾, meaning: let not the state of the worldly life deceive you, by your imagining falsehood to be truth and harm to be benefit. The attribution of deception to the worldly life is a metaphor of the intellect (majaz 'aqli), because the world is the place of deception or its cause. The real agent of deception is those who mislead them with false analogies, making the delay of a thing appear as its impossibility. So here the means of deception and its doubt are mentioned, then after it the real agent of deception is mentioned, which is "al-Gharur." "Al-Gharur" with a fatha on the ghayn refers to one who frequently deceives, and what is meant by it is Satan, through his whispering and what he places in the souls of the propagators of misguidance of doubts that disguise falsehood in a form, and what he casts into the souls of their followers so that they accept their deception.

The clause ﴿and let not the Deceiver deceive you concerning Allah﴾ is conjoined because it is included in their warning against those who cast doubts upon them, or against the illusions of their own souls which imagine falsehood to be truth so that they may confuse their opinions. And if "al-Gharur" is intended as Satan or what includes him, then that is even stronger in warning, because of the established enmity of Satan toward man, as He said: ﴿O children of Adam, let not Satan tempt you as he removed your parents from Paradise﴾ [al-A'raf: 27], and He said ﴿Indeed, Satan is an enemy to you, so take him as an enemy﴾ [Fatir: 6]; so there is in the warning a tinge of repulsion.

The (ba') in His saying ﴿let not the Deceiver deceive you concerning Allah﴾ is like the (ba') in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿O mankind, what has deceived you concerning your Lord, the Generous?﴾ [al-Infitar: 6]. Al-Zamakhshari, in al-Kashshaf, in Surat al-Infitar, established the meaning of the (ba') in a way that requires that it be causal (sababiyya), and necessarily the cause is an aspect of Allah's affairs that suits the context, not the essence of Allah, Exalted is He. What suits the context here is that the prohibition concerns not being deluded by what deception embellishes for the polytheists, such as the illusion that the idols are their intercessors with Allah in this world, and their conviction that if the Resurrection were established, against what they consider a weak possibility, their idols would intercede for them on that day; or that the Deceiver deceives them by saying that if Allah wished to resurrect people as the Messenger ﷺ says, He would resurrect their fathers while they look on; or that he deceives them by saying that if Allah wished to resurrect people He would hasten that for them, which is what Allah related of them: ﴿And they say, "When is this promise, if you should be truthful?"﴾ [Yunus: 48]. All of that is deception for them, caused by aspects of Allah, Exalted is He. In this is what clarifies the meaning of the (ba') in His saying ﴿and let not the Deceiver deceive you concerning Allah﴾. A similar expression occurs in Surat al-Hadid. This usage of transitivizing the verb "gharra" with (ba') is close to its transitivity with (min) of origin in the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

Did your love for me, that it would kill me, deceive you?
That is: let not your love for me, that it would kill me, deceive you regarding my dealing with you.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 31, verse 34 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Indeed, Allah has knowledge of the Hour, and He sends down the rain, and He knows what is in the wombs. No soul knows what it will earn tomorrow, and no soul knows in what land it will die. Indeed, Allah is All-Knowing, All-Aware.﴾

Among their delusions in denying the Resurrection was that they took the absence of an announced time for it as a sign that it would not occur. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They say, "When is this promise, if you are truthful?"﴾ [Yunus: 48], and He said: ﴿And what will make you know? Perhaps the Hour is near.﴾ [al-Shura: 17] ﴿Those who do not believe in it seek to hasten it.﴾ [al-Shura: 18]. So when the mention of the Day of Resurrection had occurred in the verses before it, this verse followed it with the statement that only Allah knows the time of the Hour.

The sentence ﴿Indeed, Allah has knowledge of the Hour﴾ is a resumptive sentence of explanation (isti'naf bayani), because it comes as an answer to a question presumed to be in people's minds. The four sentences that follow it are an inclusion (idmaj), gathering their counterparts in order to teach the community. Al-Wahidi and al-Baghawi said that a man from the Muharib of Khasafa, one of the desert dwellers, whom al-Zamakhshari in al-Kashshaf named al-Harith ibn 'Amr (the name in al-Qurtubi's tafsir and in al-Wahidi's Asbab al-Nuzul is al-Warith ibn 'Amr ibn Harithah), came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: "When is the Hour? Our lands have become barren, so when will they become fertile? I have left my wife pregnant, so what will she bear? What will I earn tomorrow? And in what land will I die?" Then this verse was revealed. The chain of this report is not known. It is also attributed to 'Ikrimah and Muqatil. Even if it were authentic, it would not conflict with considering this sentence a resumptive sentence of explanation, since that is what the context requires.

The emphasis with the particle inna establishes Allah's knowledge of the time of the Hour, and this implies the certainty of its occurrence. The word ﹛'indahu﹜ ("with Him") indicates that Allah alone has this knowledge, since the sense of "with" (al-'indiyyah) is essentially exclusivity. The fronting of ﹛'inda﹜, which is an adverbial phrase predicated on the subject, gives the sense of restriction, by the indication of context that it does not merely mean nearness in rank.

The clause ﴿and He sends down the rain﴾ is coordinated to the predicate clause. The sense is: "and indeed Allah sends down the rain," and this gives the sense of restriction to the sending down of rain. The intended meaning is also that He has knowledge of the time of the rain's descent. It is not merely the informing that He sends down rain, because that is not something they deny. Rather, the clause is phrased with the present verb so that, along with the indication that knowledge of it belongs to Him alone, there is the expression of favour through that known matter, which is a blessing.

The choice of the present verb indicates that He renews the sending down of rain time after time when the land is in need. We do not follow those who estimated the phrase as ﹛yunazzilu al-ghayth﹜ with the implied verbal particle ﹛an﹜ (that), in the manner of the verse of Tarafah:

*Ala ayyuha 'l-zajiri 'ahdur al-waghā*
*(Oh you who would restrain me, let me attend the fray)*

The difference between the two positions in eloquence is great. Since this has come as a coordinated element within a list of restriction, the placement of the verb as a predicate reporting on a fronted subject gives restriction through context. So the meaning is: He alone is independent in knowing the time of the descent of rain, whether near or far, and in fixing its time.

It is coordinated to it: ﴿and He knows what is in the wombs﴾, meaning He alone is independent in knowing all of its stages, from a drop of semen, to a clot, to a lump of flesh, then whether it is male or female, and the exact time of its delivery. The present verb is used to indicate the repetition of knowledge through the changing of those stages and states. The meaning is: He alone has knowledge of all those stages which people do not know, because it is coordinated to what the restrictive sense was intended for. Therefore the verbal predicate, which comes after the subject, gives restriction by context, as we said regarding His saying: ﴿and Allah measures the night and the day﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20].

As for His saying: ﴿No soul knows what it will earn tomorrow, and no soul knows in what land it will die﴾, it is woven in another pattern of composition. Its warp is the negation of the knowledge of any soul of its most particular states, which is the nearest of its earnings to it, on the day following the day of its reflection and consideration. Likewise, the place where its life will end, as an address to them about their lack of knowledge. So when they are in this position of little knowledge, how could they aspire to know the knowledge of the greatest events of this world, which is the event of its annihilation, its ending, and its replacement by the world of eternity? This negation of understanding these two matters regarding every soul implies the affirmation that knowledge of what every soul earns, and knowledge of the land in which every soul will die, belongs to Allah the Exalted. Thus the restriction of these two kinds of knowledge to Allah the Exalted is achieved, and these two were at the core of what was arranged with them of what preceded them.

He expressed the negation of people's knowledge with the verb of understanding (al-diraya) because understanding is a knowledge involving a process of reaching awareness of the known. Therefore the verb of understanding is not used for the knowledge of Allah the Exalted. One does not say "Allah understands such-and-such." So it indicates the negation of people's knowledge after their eagerness for it. The meaning is: no one knows that except Allah the Exalted, by the indication of their being contrasted with His saying: ﴿and He sends down the rain and He knows what is in the wombs﴾. He made the verb of understanding govern no object in two places, and the two interrogatives after it complete it. That is: you do not understand this question, meaning its answer.

The restriction of knowledge of these five matters to Allah the Exalted has been achieved through wonderful styles of the most eloquent brevity, which reach the limit of inimitability.

These five were called, in the speech of the Prophet ﷺ, the Keys of the Unseen (mafatih al-ghayb). The verse ﴿And with Him are the keys of the unseen; none knows them except Him﴾ [al-An'am: 59] was interpreted by them. In the Sahih of al-Bukhari, from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The keys of the unseen are five," then he recited ﴿Indeed, Allah has knowledge of the Hour﴾ to the end of the verse. And from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah: "[They are] five which none knows except Allah: indeed, Allah has knowledge of the Hour" as an answer to the question of Jibril: "When is the Hour?" ...

The meaning of confining the keys of the unseen to these five is that they are the hidden matters connected with the conditions of people in this world. Their being called keys indicates that they are unknown to people, and when they occur, their occurrence is like the opening of what was closed. As for the rest of the conditions of people, their hiddenness from them varies, and some of them can determine it, such as determining that a particular day is for a wedding, or a particular day is for a raid, and likewise the times of acts of worship and festivals. Similarly, correlations of times, such as: "such-and-such a day is the beginning of spring." So you will not find hidden matters, the occurrence of which no one can know, among the conditions of people in this world other than these five. As for the other worlds and the Hereafter, the matters hidden from human knowledge are many, and they have no keys of knowledge in this world.

[p. 199]

The sentence ﴿Indeed, Allah is All-Knowing, All-Aware﴾ is a fresh initial sentence (istి'naf ibtida'i), occurring in the place of a conclusion to what the preceding speech contained of refuting the doubt of the polytheists with His saying: ﴿Indeed, the promise of Allah is true, so let not the worldly life deceive you﴾ [Luqman: 33], like the position of His saying in the story of Luqman: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Subtle, All-Aware﴾ [Luqman: 16], following His saying: ﴿Indeed, if it should be the weight of a mustard seed﴾ [Luqman: 16], and the verse continues.

The meaning is: Allah is All-Knowing of the extent of His promise, All-Aware of your conditions, which is what His saying ﴿No soul knows what it will earn tomorrow﴾ etc. comprises. For this reason He combined the two attributes, "All-Knowing" and "All-Aware," because the second is more specific.

Surah al-Sajdah

The most well-known of this surah's names is "Surat al-Sajdah," and it is its shortest name. It is what is written on the line designated for the surah's name in the commonly circulated copies of the Qur'an. Al-Tirmidhi also titled it by this name in his Jami', by adding the word "surah" to "al-sajdah." It is necessary to assume the word "Alif-Lam-Mim" (Alif Lam Mim) as elided for brevity, since merely adding "surah" to "al-sajdah" does not suffice to identify this surah, because there is no prostration of recitation (sujud al-tilawah) in the Qur'an except in one of the surahs.

It is also called "Alif Lam Mim Tanzil." Al-Tirmidhi narrated from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah that the Prophet ﷺ "would not sleep until he recited Alif Lam Mim Tanzil and Tabaraka alladhi biyadihi al-mulk [al-Mulk: 1]."

It is also called "Alif Lam Mim Tanzil al-Sajdah." In the Sahih of al-Bukhari, from Abu Hurayrah: "The Prophet ﷺ used to recite on Friday in the dawn prayer Alif Lam Mim Tanzil al-Sajdah and Hal ata 'ala al-insan [al-Insan: 1]." The commentators on the Sahih of al-Bukhari said that the lam in the word "Tanzil" is vocalized with a damma, as a quotation of the wording of the Qur'an. As for the word "al-Sajdah" in this hadith, Ibn Hajar said it is in the accusative case. Al-Ayni and al-Qastallani said it is in the accusative as an explanatory apposition (atf bayan), meaning that it explains the expression "Alif Lam Mim Tanzil." This is far-fetched, because the word "al-Sajdah" is not the name of this surah except with the addition of "surah" to "al-Sajdah." So the correct view is that the word "al-Sajdah" in Abu Hurayrah's statement is in the genitive, by the annexation of the whole phrase "Alif Lam Mim Tanzil" to the word "al-Sajdah." I will explain how this annexation works.

Al-Bukhari titled it in his Sahih "Surat Tanzil al-Sajdah." The word "Tanzil" must be vocalized with a damma as a quotation of the Qur'anic wording. Thus this surah is distinguished, among the surahs that begin with "Alif Lam Mim," by the occurrence in it of a prostration of recitation.

Whoever called it "Surat al-Sajdah" intends an elided annexed noun, meaning "the surah of (Alif Lam Mim) al-Sajdah."

Whoever called it "Tanzil al-Sajdah" means "Alif Lam Mim Tanzil al-Sajdah," by taking "Alif Lam Mim Tanzil" as a compound name, then annexing it to "al-Sajdah," meaning "the very prostration," for added distinction and clarity. Otherwise, mentioning "Tanzil" suffices to distinguish it from the other surahs beginning with "Alif Lam Mim." Then "Alif Lam Mim" was dropped and "Tanzil" retained, and "Tanzil" was annexed to "al-Sajdah," as will come in explaining the naming "Alif Lam Mim Tanzil al-Sajdah."

Whoever called it "Alif Lam Mim al-Sajdah" means the annexation of "Alif Lam Mim" to "al-Sajdah" in the sense of the lam (of possession or association), making "Alif Lam Mim" a name for the surah.

Those who called it "Alif Lam Mim Tanzil al-Sajdah" did not discuss its vocalization in the commentaries on the Sahih of al-Bukhari, nor in the correct copies of the Jami' al-Sahih. It is necessary that "Alif Lam Mim" be annexed to "Tanzil," so that the whole annexed phrase is a name for this surah, with "Tanzil" vocalized with a damma as a quotation of its Qur'anic wording. This compound annexed phrase is treated as a proper name, like "'Abd Allah," and the whole of that annexed compound is treated as annexed to "al-Sajdah" by the annexation of individual nouns. This is an attested usage. Among it is the verse of Ta'abbata Sharran:

*Inni lamuhdin min thana'i fa-qasidun*
*bihi li-ibni 'ammi al-sidqi shamsi ibn Malik*

He annexed the whole phrase "ibn 'amm" (cousin) to "al-sidq" (truthfulness), and did not intend the annexation of "'amm" to "al-sidq."

Likewise is the saying of a man from the Tayy in the Hamasa anthology:

*Dawi ibn 'amm al-su'i bil-na'yi wal-ghina*
*kafa bil-ghina wal-na'yi 'anhu mudawiya*

(Treat the bad cousin with distance and wealth; wealth and distance from him suffice as a cure.)

He did not intend to describe his paternal uncle as bad, but he intended to describe the cousin as bad. So he annexed the whole phrase "ibn 'amm" to "al-su'," and a similar example is the saying of a man of the Kalb in the Hamasa:

*Hanii'an li-ibni 'ammi al-su'i anni*
*mujawiratun banī Tha'lin labūnī*

(Congratulations to the bad cousin: I am a neighbour to the Banu Tha'l, with my milk-camels.)

'Uyaynah ibn Mirdas said in the Hamasa:

*Falamma 'arftu al-ya'sa minhu wa-qad badat*
*aydi Saba al-hajati lil-mutadhakkiri*

(When I recognized despair from him, and the hands of Saba' of needs had appeared to the one who remembers.)

He annexed the whole phrase "aydi Saba'" (the scattered hands of Saba', which functions like a single word, as it became like a proverb) to "al-hajat."

One of their rajaz poets said:

*Ana ibn 'amm al-layli wa-ibnu khalihi*
*idha dujan dakhaltu fi sirbalihi*

(I am the cousin of the night and the son of its maternal uncle; when it is dark, I enter into its cloak.)

He annexed "ibn 'amm" to the word "al-layl," and annexed "ibn khal" to the pronoun of "al-layl," meaning "I mingle with the night." He does not intend the annexation of "'amm" or "khal" to "al-layl."

From this is the name of 'Abd Allah ibn Qays al-Ruqayyat: the thing annexed to "al-Ruqayyat" is the whole compound, either "'Abd Allah" or "ibn Qays," not any one of its individual words.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 31, verse 34 (part 2 of 2):

This annexation is close to the annexation of a compound number to what it is attached to while the number itself keeps its fixed form, as when you say: "Give him fifteen" (*khamsata 'ashara*).

This surah is also called (*Surat al-Madajie*, "the Surah of the Beds") because the word "beds" (*al-madajie*) occurs in His saying, ﴿Their sides forsake their beds﴾ [al-Sajda 32:16].

In the Tafsir (exegesis) of al-Qurtubi, citing the Musnad of al-Darimi, it is related that Khalid ibn Ma'dan named it (*al-Munjiyah*, "the Deliverer"). He said: "It reached me that a man used to recite it and recited nothing else, and he committed many sins. So the surah spread its wing and said: 'My Lord, forgive him, for he used to recite me often.' So the Lord interceded for him and said: 'Write for him a good deed for every sin, and raise him a degree.'" End of quotation.

Al-Tabarsi said: It is called (*Surat Sajdat Luqman*, "the Surah of the Prostration of Luqman"), because it comes after Surat Luqman, lest it be confused with (*Ha Mim al-Sajda*). That is, just as they named Surat Ha Mim al-Sajda, which is Surat Fussilat, (*Surat Sajdat al-Mu'min*, "the Surah of the Prostration of the Believer"), because it comes after (*Surat al-Mu'minun*).

It is Meccan according to the general statement of most exegetes and one of two narrations from Ibn 'Abbas. In another narration from him, three Medinan verses are excepted, namely ﴿Is he who was a believer like he who was defiantly disobedient?﴾ [al-Sajda 32:18] up to ﴿perhaps they will be guided﴾. It was said they were revealed on the day of Badr concerning 'Ali ibn Abi Talib and al-Walid ibn 'Uqba, and its refutation will come. Some added two verses: ﴿Their sides forsake their beds﴾ [al-Sajda 32:16] up to ﴿for what they used to do﴾, because of what has been narrated about the occasion of its revelation, but this is weak.

What we rely upon is that the whole surah is Meccan, and that whatever contradicts this is only an interpretation or the attachment of a particular case to a general one, as we established in the Fifth Introduction.

It was revealed after Surat al-Nahl and before Surat Nuh, and it is counted as the seventy-third in order of revelation.

Its verses are counted by the majority of counters as thirty, and the people of Basra counted them as twenty-seven.

Among the aims of this surah, the first is the highlighting of the Qur'an, that it is sent down from Allah, and the rebuke of the polytheists for their claim that it is a fabrication, since they had never before been honored by the descent of a Book.

Then the argument against the divinity of their idols, by establishing that Allah alone is the Creator of the heavens and the earth and the Manager of their affairs.

Then the mention of the Resurrection and the argument for how the human being's first creation and his offspring began, and its comparison to the revival of the earth. Included in this is that the revival of the earth is a blessing upon them, which they denied by ignoring its Giver.

Then the condemnation of those who denied it and their warning.

Then the praise of those who affirm the signs of Allah and the promise to them, and the contrast of their faith with the disbelief of the polytheists. Then the affirmation of the messengership of a great Messenger before Muhammad (ﷺ), who guided a great nation.

Then the reminder of what befell the earlier deniers, so that this would be a lesson for those present, and the threat to them of the victory granted to the believers.

It concludes with waiting for victory.

Allah commanded the Messenger (ﷺ) to turn away from them, to belittle them, and promised him that he would await His victory over them.

* * *

Among the excellences and virtues of this surah is what al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ahmad and al-Darimi narrated from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) would not sleep until he recited Alif Lam Mim, the Revelation (*Tanzil al-Sajda*) [Surat al-Sajda], and ﴿Blessed is He in whose hand is the dominion﴾ [al-Mulk 67:1]."
